sections.title: Scalar vs vector: the auto-driver test & related topics

board_events.text: Scalar vs Vector: what is missing?
Scalar = size only. Vector = size AND direction.
'Take me 4 km' is incomplete; '4 km towards Nehru Place' is a vector.
The number alone is a scalar; attach a direction and it becomes a vector.
Scalars: temperature, mass, distance, speed, bank balance.
Vectors: displacement, velocity, force, a fielder's throw.

board_events.caption: The number 4 km is a scalar; add a direction and it becomes a vector.

board_events.text: This single distinction is the seed of the whole chapter.
A vector is a portable instruction
Draw a vector as a directed segment, an arrow from tail A to head B, written $\vec{AB}$.
Arrow length is the magnitude $\lvert \vec{AB}\rvert$; the arrowhead is the direction.
The instruction 'move this far, in this direction' does not care where you start.
Same length and same direction means the same vector, wherever it sits.
So we can freely slide a vector to set it tail-to-head with another.
Equality needs BOTH: same magnitude AND same direction, never one alone.

board_events.caption: Two arrows of equal length and direction are the same vector, wherever they are drawn.

board_events.text: Resolving into components
Grid directions: 'go 3 blocks east, 2 north, 1 floor up' fixes where you land.
Three perpendicular unit vectors: $\hat i$ (x-axis), $\hat j$ (y-axis), $\hat k$ (z-axis), each of length 1.

board_events.latex: \vec r = x\,\hat i + y\,\hat j + z\,\hat k

board_events.text: Here $x, y, z$ are the scalar components of $\vec r$.
The arrow and the triple $(x, y, z)$ are two faces of the same object.

board_events.caption: Any vector r resolves into components along the i, j, k axes.
board_events.svg: <svg font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" viewBox="0 0 420 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah3" markerWidth="10" markerHeight="10" refX="8" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L8,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#333"/></marker></defs><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="330" y2="200" stroke="#333" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#ah3)"/><text x="335" y="205" font-size="13" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif">x</text><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="60" y2="40" stroke="#333" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#ah3)"/><text x="48" y="35" font-size="13" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif">z</text><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="180" y2="250" stroke="#333" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#ah3)"/><text x="185" y="255" font-size="13" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif">y</text><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="250" y2="90" stroke="#c0392b" stroke-width="2.5" marker-end="url(#ah3)"/><text x="240" y="80" font-size="14" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" fill="#c0392b">r = x i + y j + z k</text><text x="150" y="218" font-size="11" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif">x component</text></svg>

board_events.text: Every vector in space can be written this one way, which makes vectors computable.
Four assumptions exams love to attack
1. A position vector is NOT free, it is tied to the origin O.
2. Equality needs BOTH: same magnitude and same direction.
3. The zero vector $\vec 0$ has magnitude 0 and no definite direction.
'The direction cosines of $\vec 0$' is a meaningless phrase.
4. A unit vector needs a non-zero vector, since we divide by the magnitude.
Most 'silly' mistakes here are really a violation of one of these four.
Drag all four into the light before every problem.
The vector zoo
Zero vector $\vec 0$: magnitude 0, direction undefined.
Unit vector: magnitude exactly 1.
Equal vectors: same magnitude AND same direction.
Negative of $\vec a$: same magnitude, opposite direction, written $-\vec a$.
Collinear / parallel: $\vec a = \lambda \vec b$ for some scalar $\lambda$.
Coplanar: all lie in one plane. Position vector: drawn from O to a fixed point.
Know each by its ONE defining property, that is what MCQs test.
Magnitude and the unit vector
For $\vec r = x\hat i + y\hat j + z\hat k$, the magnitude is the 3-D Pythagoras length.
$\lvert \vec r\rvert \ge 0$; it equals zero only for the zero vector.
A unit vector has magnitude exactly 1, keeping direction and dropping size.
Defined only when $\vec a \neq \vec 0$, you cannot divide by zero.
To get a vector of magnitude $k$ along $\vec a$, scale its unit vector: $k\,\hat a$.
Position vector and joining two points
Position vector of $P(x, y, z)$ relative to origin O:

board_events.latex: \vec{OP} = x\,\hat i + y\,\hat j + z\,\hat k, \qquad \lvert \vec{OP}\rvert = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}

board_events.text: If A, B have position vectors $\vec a, \vec b$, the vector from A to B is head minus tail:
$\vec{AB} = -\,\vec{BA}$, subtraction order is everything.
Always head minus tail; reverse it and every sign flips.
This one rule powers the section formula, collinearity, and areas later.
Scalar multiplication
Multiply $\vec a$ by a scalar $\lambda$, it stretches or flips, never rotates sideways.
If $\lambda > 0$: same direction. If $\lambda < 0$: opposite direction.
If $\lambda = 0$: you get the zero vector $\vec 0$.
Magnitude scales by $\lvert\lambda\rvert$, the absolute value, never by $\lambda$ itself.
This is exactly how we rescale a unit vector to any length.
Stretch, shrink, or reverse, but direction stays on the same line.
Direction cosines
Cosines of the angles $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ a vector makes with the positive x, y, z axes.
For $\vec r$ with magnitude $r$: divide each component by $r$.
If three numbers' squares do not sum to 1, they are NOT direction cosines.

board_events.caption: The vector r makes angles alpha, beta, gamma with the three axes.

board_events.text: Direction ratios
Any three numbers $(a, b, c)$ proportional to the direction cosines.
The scalar components $(x, y, z)$ are themselves a valid set of direction ratios.
Direction cosines are unique (up to sign); direction ratios are NOT unique.
$(2, -1, 2)$ and $(4, -2, 4)$ describe the same direction.
To turn ratios into cosines: divide by $\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}$.
Remember: DR means Ratio-only; DC means Divided-by-magnitude.
Collinearity condition
Three points A, B, C are collinear when they lie on one straight line.
Equivalently, $\vec b - \vec a$ and $\vec c - \vec a$ are parallel.
One vector is a scalar multiple of the other, that IS collinearity.
This turns a geometry question into one quick proportionality check.
Used constantly in 'find k so that A, B, C are collinear' problems.

board_events.caption: Three collinear points: AB and AC lie along the same line.

segments.text: <curious>Let me start with a puzzle. You hop into an auto at Connaught Place and say, take me four kilometres. Where does the driver go?
The problem is that a plain number carries only size. Four kilometres is a scalar, it tells you how much but never which way.
The instant you say four kilometres towards Nehru Place, you have handed over a vector, a quantity with both a magnitude and a direction.
Hold on to this: the bare number is a scalar, and the moment you attach a direction to it, it becomes a vector.
So which quantities are scalars? Temperature, mass, distance, speed, even your bank balance, each is fully pinned down by a single number.
And vectors? Displacement, velocity, force, and a fielder's throw in cricket, a throw of eighty kilometres an hour means nothing until you add, towards the stumps.
Picture it on the board: four kilometres by itself sits as a lonely number, while the two arrows leave the same point heading to completely different corners of the city.
That one distinction, size alone versus size with direction, is the seed from which this entire chapter grows.
Here is the mental picture that makes vectors easy: a vector is simply an instruction, move this far, in this direction.
We draw that instruction as an arrow. It runs from a tail, point A, to a head, point B, and we write it A B with an arrow on top.
The arrow does two jobs at once: its length shows the magnitude, and its arrowhead shows the direction.
Now the crucial twist, the instruction does not care where you begin. Two hundred metres due east is the same journey from any gate of the colony.
So remember this firmly: two arrows with the same length and the same direction are the very same vector, no matter where they sit on the page.
That freedom is powerful. It lets us slide a vector across the diagram and set it tail-to-head against another one when we add them.
But equality is strict, it needs both conditions. Same length alone is not enough, and same direction alone is not enough, you need both together.
On the board those two arrows sit in different places yet point the same way with equal length, so they are, truly, one and the same vector.
We have an arrow, but arrows are hard to compute with, so we translate every vector into numbers by resolving it into components.
Think of giving directions on a city grid: go three blocks east, then two blocks north, then up one floor. Those three numbers fix your endpoint exactly.
In maths the three grid directions are the unit vectors, i-hat along the x-axis, j-hat along the y-axis, and k-hat along the z-axis, each exactly one unit long.
So any vector r becomes x times i-hat, plus y times j-hat, plus z times k-hat.
Those coefficients x, y and z are called the scalar components of the vector.
Here is the key idea: the arrow you draw and the triple x, y, z are just two faces of the very same object.
On the board you can see the arrow reaching into space while its shadow drops onto each axis to read off x, y and z.
Because every vector in space can be written this single way, components are what let us actually calculate with vectors.
Before we compute anything, let me drag four quiet assumptions into the light, because exams attack them directly.
First, a position vector is not a free vector. It is deliberately anchored to the origin O; slide it and you change what it means.
Second, equality is a double condition. Two vectors are equal only when they share both magnitude and direction; parallel but different length does not count.
Third, the zero vector has magnitude zero and, importantly, no definite direction at all.
So a phrase like the direction cosines of the zero vector is simply meaningless, there is no direction to take cosines of.
Fourth, a unit vector can only be built from a non-zero vector, because the recipe divides by the magnitude, and you cannot divide by zero.
Here is the pattern to notice: most so-called silly mistakes in this topic are really a quiet violation of one of these four rules.
So keep all four in view before you start any problem, they catch errors before they happen.
Let me introduce the whole cast of characters, the vector zoo, because exams test whether you know each by its one defining property.
The zero vector: magnitude zero, and direction undefined. It is the odd one out that breaks many careless statements.
The unit vector: the only property that matters is magnitude exactly one, it is pure direction.
Equal vectors: same magnitude and same direction, both together, as we already stressed.
The negative of a vector a: same length, but pointing exactly the opposite way, and we write it minus a.
Collinear or parallel vectors: one is a scalar multiple of the other, a equals lambda times b for some number lambda.
Coplanar vectors all lie in, or parallel to, a single plane; and a position vector is the special one drawn from the origin to a fixed point.
For the exam, learn each animal by its single defining property, that one line is exactly what the multiple choice questions probe.
Now we pin a vector down with numbers, and the first thing we want is its length, its magnitude.
If the vector is x i plus y j plus z k, its length is just the three dimensional version of Pythagoras' theorem.
Written out: the magnitude of r equals the square root of x squared plus y squared plus z squared. Square each component, add them, take the root.
One quiet property, this length is never negative, and it hits exactly zero only for the zero vector.
Very often we do not want the size, only the direction. For that we build a unit vector, magnitude exactly one, pure direction.
The recipe is simple: divide the vector by its own magnitude. a-hat equals a over the magnitude of a.
<whisper>But watch the fine print, this is defined only when a is non-zero, because dividing by zero magnitude is meaningless.
And if you need a vector of some length k pointing along a, just scale the unit vector by k, that is, k times a-hat.
Two closely related formulas now, the position vector of a point, and the vector that joins two points.
The position vector of a point P with coordinates x, y, z is measured from the origin O.
It is simply x i-hat plus y j-hat plus z k-hat, and its magnitude is the square root of x squared plus y squared plus z squared, the same Pythagoras length as before.
Now if A and B have position vectors a and b, how do we get the arrow from A to B? Head minus tail.
So the vector A B equals b minus a, the head's position vector minus the tail's.
<whisper>And here is the trap: A B equals minus B A. The order of subtraction is everything.
Say it like a mantra, always head minus tail. Reverse the order and every single sign flips on you.
This one humble rule quietly powers the section formula, the collinearity test, and the area formulas you will meet later.
Scalar multiplication is the simplest operation, take a vector a and multiply it by a plain number lambda.
Geometrically it only stretches or flips the arrow along its own line; it never swings it sideways to a new direction.
The magnitude rule: the length of lambda a equals the absolute value of lambda, times the length of a.
The direction depends on the sign. If lambda is positive the direction is unchanged; if lambda is negative the arrow reverses.
And if lambda is exactly zero, the whole thing collapses to the zero vector.
Notice carefully, the length scales by the absolute value of lambda, not lambda itself, because a length can never be negative.
This is precisely the tool we used a moment ago to rescale a unit vector to any length we like.
So: stretch, shrink, or reverse, but the direction always stays on the same straight line.
Direction cosines are how we capture a vector's direction as three clean numbers.
They are the cosines of the three angles, alpha, beta and gamma, that the vector makes with the positive x, y and z axes.
We name them l, m and n: l is cosine alpha, m is cosine beta, n is cosine gamma.
To compute them for a vector r of magnitude r, you just divide each component by that magnitude.
So l is x over r, m is y over r, and n is z over r, you are simply reading off the unit vector's components.
And they obey a beautiful identity: l squared plus m squared plus n squared equals one. Always.
<curious>Why care? Because if someone hands you three numbers whose squares do not add to one, they cannot possibly be direction cosines, so reject them instantly.
On the board you can see the single arrow leaning against all three axes, one angle to each, that is the whole picture.
Direction ratios are the relaxed cousins of direction cosines.
They are any three numbers a, b, c that are proportional to the direction cosines, the proportions matter, not the exact size.
The link is this chain of equal ratios: l over a equals m over b equals n over c equals one over the root of a squared plus b squared plus c squared.
A handy fact: the plain scalar components x, y, z of a vector already form a perfectly valid set of direction ratios.
But here is the key contrast, direction cosines are unique, up to an overall sign, while direction ratios are not unique at all.
For instance two, minus one, two, and four, minus two, four, describe exactly the same direction, just scaled differently.
To convert ratios into cosines, normalise: divide each ratio by the root of a squared plus b squared plus c squared.
Lock in the memory hook, D R means ratio only, D C means divided by magnitude.
Collinearity is just a fancy word for three points sitting on a single straight line.
Take three points A, B and C, when are they collinear?
The test is clean: the vector A B must be a scalar multiple of the vector A C. That is, A B equals lambda times A C for some number lambda.
Equivalently, b minus a and c minus a point along the same line, they are parallel.
The whole idea is that one of these vectors is simply a stretched or shrunk copy of the other; that is exactly what collinearity means.
The payoff is that a geometry question collapses into a single, quick proportionality check, no diagram gymnastics needed.
You will use this constantly in problems that say, find the value of k so that A, B and C are collinear.
On the board all three points sit on one line, with A B and A C pointing the same way, one just longer than the other.

We name them l, m and n: l is cosine alpha, m is cosine beta, n is cosine gamma.
To compute them for a vector r of magnitude r, you just divide each component by that magnitude.
So l is x over r, m is y over r, and n is z over r, you are simply reading off the unit vector's components.
And they obey a beautiful identity: l squared plus m squared plus n squared equals one. Always.
<curious>Why care? Because if someone hands you three numbers whose squares do not add to one, they cannot possibly be direction cosines, so reject them instantly.
On the board you can see the single arrow leaning against all three axes, one angle to each, that is the whole picture.
Direction ratios are the relaxed cousins of direction cosines.
They are any three numbers a, b, c that are proportional to the direction cosines, the proportions matter, not the exact size.
The link is this chain of equal ratios: l over a equals m over b equals n over c equals one over the root of a squared plus b squared plus c squared.
A handy fact: the plain scalar components x, y, z of a vector already form a perfectly valid set of direction ratios.
But here is the key contrast, direction cosines are unique, up to an overall sign, while direction ratios are not unique at all.
For instance two, minus one, two, and four, minus two, four, describe exactly the same direction, just scaled differently.
To convert ratios into cosines, normalise: divide each ratio by the root of a squared plus b squared plus c squared.
Lock in the memory hook, D R means ratio only, D C means divided by magnitude.
Collinearity is just a fancy word for three points sitting on a single straight line.
Take three points A, B and C, when are they collinear?
The test is clean: the vector A B must be a scalar multiple of the vector A C. That is, A B equals lambda times A C for some number lambda.
Equivalently, b minus a and c minus a point along the same line, they are parallel.
The whole idea is that one of these vectors is simply a stretched or shrunk copy of the other; that is exactly what collinearity means.
The payoff is that a geometry question collapses into a single, quick proportionality check, no diagram gymnastics needed.
You will use this constantly in problems that say, find the value of k so that A, B and C are collinear.
On the board all three points sit on one line, with A B and A C pointing the same way, one just longer than the other.

sections.title: Proof: why the DC squares sum to one & related topics

board_events.text: Proof: why the DC squares sum to one
Claim: for any non-zero vector, $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$.
Let $\vec r = x\hat i + y\hat j + z\hat k$ with $r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2} > 0$.
Square each and add; the denominators are all $r^2$.
The numerator collapses to $r^2$ because $r^2 = x^2+y^2+z^2$ by definition.
Reading it: a valid direction is exactly one whose DC-squares total 1.
Proof: the collinearity test
Claim: A, B, C are collinear iff $\vec b - \vec a = \lambda(\vec c - \vec a)$ for some $\lambda$.
A, B, C on one line means $\vec{AB}$ and $\vec{AC}$ run along the same line.
Two vectors along one line means one is a scalar multiple of the other.
Substitute $\vec{AB} = \vec b - \vec a$ and $\vec{AC} = \vec c - \vec a$.
The 'iff' runs both ways: parallel-through-A is the same as collinear.
Example: unit vector, then scale to 35
Given $\vec a = 6\hat i - 2\hat j + 3\hat k$. Find $\hat a$, then the vector of magnitude 35 along it.
Scale the unit vector by 35 to get the required vector.

board_events.latex: 35\,\hat a = 5\left(6\hat i - 2\hat j + 3\hat k\right) = 30\hat i - 10\hat j + 15\hat k

board_events.text: Two steps every time: normalise to a unit vector, then rescale.
Example: the QP order trap
$P(2, -1, 3)$ and $Q(5, 3, -1)$. Find the unit vector along $\vec{QP}$.
Trap: computing $\vec{PQ}$ flips every sign, and is marked wrong.
$\vec{QP}$ goes from Q to P: head P minus tail Q.

board_events.latex: \vec{QP} = (2-5)\hat i + (-1-3)\hat j + (3-(-1))\hat k = -3\hat i - 4\hat j + 4\hat k

board_events.text: MCQ shortcut: fix signs from Q to P and spot the $\sqrt{41}$ denominator first.
Example: the centroid from medians
Triangle $ABC$ with vertices $\vec a, \vec b, \vec c$. D is midpoint of BC; P divides median AD in $2:1$ from A.
The result is completely symmetric in $\vec a, \vec b, \vec c$.
Starting from any vertex's median gives the identical point.

board_events.text: Pitfalls and the squares-sum-to-one gatekeeper
DR vs DC mix-up: DRs are any proportional triple; DCs satisfy $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$.
If it says 'direction cosines', you MUST divide by the magnitude.
Subtraction order: always $\vec{AB} = \vec b - \vec a$. Writing $\vec a - \vec b$ gives $\vec{BA}$.
Internal vs external: internal has $+$ and $m+n$; external has $-$ and $m-n$.
Unit-vector slip: divide by $\lvert \vec r\rvert$, never by $\lvert \vec r\rvert^2$.
Pro-tip: to test any claimed DCs or unit vector, square the three and add, expect 1.
One check kills two or three MCQ distractors in seconds.
Two ways to multiply two vectors
One asks 'how much do they agree in direction?' and answers with a number (dot product).
The other asks 'how much do they spread apart?' and answers with a new vector (cross product).
Dot: maximal when parallel, zero when perpendicular.
Cross: zero when parallel, maximal when perpendicular.
Wherever one is large, the other tends to be small, mirror-image questions.
Together they fix how two vectors are oriented relative to each other.
Master both and you own most of the chapter's marks.
The dot product: overlap
Push a handcart down a lane at a slight angle.
Only the part of your push ALONG the lane moves the cart forward.
The dot product measures that useful overlap between two directions.
Same direction: maximum overlap. Perpendicular: zero overlap.
The result is a single number, 'amount of agreement' is a quantity, not a direction.

board_events.text: Think of it as the shadow one vector casts on another.
The cross product: spread and twist
Open a heavy almirah door: push near the hinge, little turn; push at the far edge, big turn.
The turning effect is largest when your push is perpendicular to the door.
The cross product is zero when vectors are parallel, maximal when perpendicular.
It produces a NEW vector, perpendicular to both, along the axis of their spread.
Right-hand rule: curl fingers from a to b; the thumb points along $\vec a \times \vec b$.
$\vec a \times \vec b = -\,\vec b \times \vec a$, reverse the order and the thumb flips.

board_events.text: Four traps in the two products
For non-zero vectors, $\vec a \cdot \vec b = 0$ means perpendicular.
But $\vec a \times \vec b = \vec 0$ means parallel (collinear).
Confusing these two zero-conditions is the single most common error here.
The cross product is NOT commutative: $\vec a \times \vec b = -\,\vec b \times \vec a$.
There is no vector division; from $\vec a \cdot \vec b$ alone you cannot recover $\vec b$.
A scalar vs a vector: $\vec a \cdot \vec b$ is a number; $\vec a \times \vec b$ is a vector.
Write one where the other belongs and it is a conceptual, not arithmetic, slip.

segments.text: Let us actually prove the identity we just met, that the direction cosines of any non-zero vector square to one.
The claim, precisely: for any non-zero vector, l squared plus m squared plus n squared equals one.
Start with r equals x i-hat plus y j-hat plus z k-hat, and let its magnitude r be the root of x squared plus y squared plus z squared, which is strictly positive.
By definition the direction cosines are the components divided by that length: l is x over r, m is y over r, n is z over r.
Now square each of the three and add them. Since each is divided by r, every denominator is r squared.
So the sum is x squared plus y squared plus z squared, all over r squared, which is r squared over r squared, and that is one.
The numerator collapses to r squared precisely because r squared was defined as x squared plus y squared plus z squared, the magnitude definition does the work.
Read the result plainly: a legitimate direction is exactly one whose three cosine-squares total one. It is the fastest sanity check in the topic.
This proof is short, and it makes the collinearity test feel inevitable.
The claim: points A, B and C are collinear if and only if b minus a equals lambda times c minus a, for some scalar lambda.
Start from the geometry. A, B and C lying on one straight line simply means the arrows A B and A C run along the very same line.
But two vectors lying along one line is precisely the statement that one is a scalar multiple of the other.
So A B equals lambda times A C; that scalar lambda is the whole content of the condition.
Now substitute the head-minus-tail forms: A B is b minus a, and A C is c minus a.
That gives b minus a equals lambda times the quantity c minus a, exactly the condition we claimed.
And note the if-and-only-if runs both directions: being parallel through the common point A is the same thing as being collinear.
Let us put the magnitude and unit vector machinery to work on a clean board-level problem.
We are given a equals six i-hat minus two j-hat plus three k-hat, and we want its unit vector, and then a vector of magnitude thirty five in the same direction.
Step one, the magnitude: root of six squared plus minus-two squared plus three squared, which is root of thirty six plus four plus nine, equal to root forty nine, that is seven.
Step two, the unit vector: divide a by seven, giving one seventh of the bracket six i-hat minus two j-hat plus three k-hat.
Step three, we want length thirty five, so we simply scale that unit vector by thirty five.
Thirty five over seven is five, so the answer is five times the bracket, thirty i-hat minus ten j-hat plus fifteen k-hat.
And a quick check seals it: root of thirty squared plus ten squared plus fifteen squared is root twelve twenty five, which is exactly thirty five. It works.
The rhythm is always the same two steps, normalise to a unit vector first, then rescale to the length you need.
This one is a classic trap, and reading the order carefully is the whole battle.
We have P at two, minus one, three, and Q at five, three, minus one, and we want the unit vector along Q P.
<whisper>Here is the trap, under pressure students compute P Q instead of Q P, and every sign flips, so the answer is marked wrong.
So read it slowly. Q P runs from Q to P, which means head P minus tail Q.
Component by component: two minus five is minus three, minus one minus three is minus four, and three minus minus one is plus four, so Q P is minus three i-hat minus four j-hat plus four k-hat.
Its magnitude is the root of nine plus sixteen plus sixteen, which is root forty one.
So the unit vector is one over root forty one, times the bracket minus three i-hat minus four j-hat plus four k-hat.
In a multiple choice setting, decide the signs from Q to P and spot the root forty one denominator first; any option with the wrong signs or a different denominator is gone instantly.
Now a J E E Advanced flavoured proof that shows the sheer economy of the vector method.
In triangle A B C with vertices a, b and c, let D be the midpoint of B C, and let P divide the median A D in the ratio two to one, measured from A.
First locate D by the midpoint formula, it is b plus c over two.
Now divide A D in two to one from A to D. Plugging into the section formula, the two-thirds point works out to a plus b plus c, all over three.
Look closely at that result, it is completely symmetric in a, b and c; not one vertex is special.
So if we had instead started from the median at B, or at C, the identical algebra would hand us the very same point.
That common point is the centroid G, with position vector a plus b plus c over three, and it proves all three medians are concurrent.
On the board the three medians cross at a single G, which divides each median two to one from its vertex, three lines of vector algebra doing what coordinate geometry needs a page for.
Let me close this subtopic with the mistakes that quietly cost marks, and one pro-tip that hands them back.
The commonest error is mixing up direction ratios and direction cosines, ratios are any proportional triple, but cosines must satisfy the squares-sum-to-one identity.
So whenever the question actually says direction cosines, you must divide by the magnitude; do not stop at the ratios.
Second, the subtraction order, always head minus tail, A B equals b minus a. Writing a minus b silently computes B A and flips every sign.
Third, internal versus external section formula: internal carries a plus sign with denominator m plus n, while external carries a minus with denominator m minus n.
Fourth, the unit vector slip, you divide by the magnitude, never by its square; the denominator is the length itself.
And now the pro-tip that pays off constantly, whenever an option claims to be direction cosines or a unit vector, just square the three numbers and add.
<excited>If you do not land on one, eliminate that option on sight; this single check often kills two or three distractors in seconds.
<curious>Here is a question you might not have asked: how do you multiply two vectors? It turns out there are two completely different answers.
The first multiplication asks, how much do these two vectors agree in direction? And it answers with a plain number, the dot, or scalar, product.
The second asks, how much do these two vectors spread apart? And it answers with a brand new vector, the cross, or vector, product.
The dot product is largest when the vectors point the same way, and it drops to zero when they are perpendicular.
The cross product is the exact opposite, zero when they are parallel, and largest when they cross at a right angle.
So they are mirror-image questions: wherever one is large, the other tends to be small.
Between them, these two products tell you everything about how two vectors are oriented relative to each other.
This is one of the highest-yield subtopics in the chapter, so master both products and you own most of its marks.
Let us build real intuition for the dot product, because a formula without a picture is easy to forget.
Picture pushing a loaded handcart, a thela, down a straight market lane, and you shove at a slight angle to the lane.
Only the part of your push that points along the lane actually moves the cart forward; the sideways part is completely wasted.
The dot product measures exactly that useful overlap between two directions, how much of one lines up with the other.
When the two vectors point the same way the overlap is maximum, and when they are perpendicular there is no overlap at all, so the dot product is zero.
And crucially the result is a single number, a scalar, because amount of agreement is just a quantity, not a direction.
On the board you can see vector a dropping a perpendicular shadow onto vector b, and that shadow length is the heart of the dot product.
So carry this image: the dot product is the shadow one vector casts on another.
The cross product needs a different picture, think of turning, not overlap.
Picture opening a heavy almirah door. Push right next to the hinge and almost nothing happens; push at the far edge, perpendicular to the door, and it swings open easily.
So the turning effect depends on how perpendicular your push is to the door, and it is strongest at a right angle.
The cross product captures exactly this: it is zero when the two vectors are parallel, and largest when they are perpendicular.
But unlike the dot product it produces a brand new vector, one pointing perpendicular to both, straight along the axis of their spread, like the hinge sticking out of the door.
Its direction is fixed by the right-hand rule: curl the fingers of your right hand from a toward b, and your thumb points along a cross b.
And here is why order matters: reverse it, and your thumb flips, so a cross b equals minus b cross a.
On the board, a and b lie in the flat plane while a cross b stands straight up out of it, that is the whole geometry.
Before the formulas, four traps that this subtopic sets again and again.
First, the word zero means opposite things for the two products. For non-zero vectors, a dot b equal to zero means the vectors are perpendicular.
But a cross b equal to the zero vector means the vectors are parallel, or collinear.
Confusing these two zero-conditions is, truly, the single most common error in the whole subtopic.
Second, the cross product is not commutative, a cross b equals minus b cross a, while the dot product is commutative.
Third, there is no such thing as vector division. From the number a dot b alone, you simply cannot recover the vector b.
Fourth, keep the outputs straight: a dot b is a number, a scalar, while a cross b is a vector.
Writing one where the other belongs, saying a dot b is a vector for instance, is a conceptual mistake, not just an arithmetic one.
Now the precise definitions, starting with the dot product, in two equivalent forms.
Take two vectors with an angle theta between them, where theta runs from zero to pi.
The geometric definition is a dot b equals the magnitude of a, times the magnitude of b, times cosine theta.
For calculation we prefer components. Write a as a-one i-hat plus a-two j-hat plus a-three k-hat, and b similarly.
Then a dot b is simply a-one b-one plus a-two b-two plus a-three b-three, multiply matching components and add.
Notice the result is a scalar, a single number, exactly as the overlap picture promised.
A neat special case: a dotted with itself gives the magnitude of a, squared, since the angle is zero and cosine is one.
And the basis rule underneath it all: i-hat dot i-hat is one, while i-hat dot j-hat is zero, and so on for every pair.

board_events.text: Angle between vectors, and projection
Rearrange the definition to read the angle:
Scalar projection of $\vec a$ on $\vec b$, how much of a lies along b:
Projection VECTOR (with direction): $\dfrac{\vec a \cdot \vec b}{|\vec b|^2}\,\vec b$.
Divide by the vector you project ONTO, its magnitude, not the other's.

board_events.text: Key properties of the dot product
Commutative: $\vec a \cdot \vec b = \vec b \cdot \vec a$.
Distributive: $\vec a \cdot (\vec b + \vec c) = \vec a \cdot \vec b + \vec a \cdot \vec c$.
Perpendicularity: for non-zero vectors, $\vec a \cdot \vec b = 0 \iff \vec a \perp \vec b$.
A zero dot product is the cleanest test for a right angle.
Sign reads the angle: positive is acute, zero is right, negative is obtuse.
These few rules let you manipulate dot products like ordinary algebra.
Cross product: definition and determinant
With $\hat n$ the unit vector perpendicular to both (right-hand rule):
Magnitude alone: $|\vec a \times \vec b| = |\vec a|\,|\vec b|\sin\theta$.
Determinant (component) form:

board_events.latex: \vec a \times \vec b = \begin{vmatrix} \hat i & \hat j & \hat k \\ a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \end{vmatrix}
\vec a \times \vec b = (a_2 b_3 - a_3 b_2)\hat i - (a_1 b_3 - a_3 b_1)\hat j + (a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1)\hat k

board_events.text: The result is a vector; the middle ($\hat j$) term carries a minus sign.
Cross product geometry: areas
The magnitude $|\vec a \times \vec b|$ equals the area of the parallelogram framed by a and b.
Unit vector perpendicular to both a and b:
The $\pm$ is real: two opposite normals are both perpendicular to the plane.

board_events.caption: a and b span a parallelogram whose area is the cross-product magnitude.

board_events.text: Cross product properties and the complementary pair
Anti-commutative: $\vec a \times \vec b = -\,\vec b \times \vec a$.
Distributive: $\vec a \times (\vec b + \vec c) = \vec a \times \vec b + \vec a \times \vec c$.
Parallelism: for non-zero vectors, $\vec a \times \vec b = \vec 0 \iff \vec a \parallel \vec b$.
Basis (cyclic): $\hat i \times \hat j = \hat k$, $\hat j \times \hat k = \hat i$, $\hat k \times \hat i = \hat j$.
Dot peaks at $\theta = 0$; cross peaks at $\theta = 90^\circ$, perfectly complementary.

board_events.text: Proof: Lagrange's identity
Claim: $(\vec a \cdot \vec b)^2 + |\vec a \times \vec b|^2 = |\vec a|^2 |\vec b|^2$.
Let $\theta$ be the angle. Then $\vec a \cdot \vec b = |\vec a||\vec b|\cos\theta$.
And $|\vec a \times \vec b| = |\vec a||\vec b|\sin\theta$.

board_events.latex: (\vec a \cdot \vec b)^2 + |\vec a \times \vec b|^2 = |\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta)
(\vec a \cdot \vec b)^2 + |\vec a \times \vec b|^2 = |\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2

board_events.text: The Pythagorean identity $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$ closes it.
Payoff: get $|\vec a \times \vec b|$ from $\vec a \cdot \vec b$ without ever finding the angle.
Example: dot product, angle, projection
$\vec a = 2\hat i + 3\hat j + \hat k$, $\vec b = \hat i - 2\hat j + 2\hat k$. Find $\vec a \cdot \vec b$, the angle, and proj of a on b.
Magnitudes: $|\vec a| = \sqrt{14}$, $|\vec b| = 3$.
Negative dot product, obtuse angle, negative projection, all consistent.
One dot product feeds all three answers.
Example: perpendicular vs parallel
$\vec a = \lambda\hat i + 2\hat j - 3\hat k$, $\vec b = 3\hat i - \hat j + 2\hat k$. Find $\lambda$ for (i) perpendicular, (ii) parallel.
Trap: perpendicular uses the DOT; parallel uses proportional components.
(i) Perpendicular means $\vec a \cdot \vec b = 0$:
(ii) Parallel means components proportional: $\dfrac{\lambda}{3} = \dfrac{2}{-1} = \dfrac{-3}{2}$.
The last two are unequal, so NO $\lambda$ makes them parallel.
Example: triangle area and perpendicular unit vector
Sides from vertex A: $\vec a = 3\hat i + \hat j - 2\hat k$, $\vec b = \hat i - 3\hat j + 4\hat k$.
Perpendicular unit vector = $\pm$ (cross product) divided by (its magnitude):
Watch the minus on the $\hat j$ cofactor: $-(12+2) = -14$.
Example: Lagrange identity and diagonals
Given $|\vec a| = 5$, $|\vec b| = 4$, $\vec a \cdot \vec b = 10$. Find $|\vec a \times \vec b|$ and the parallelogram area from diagonals $\vec a + \vec b$, $\vec a - \vec b$.
Area from diagonals: $\tfrac{1}{2}|\vec d_1 \times \vec d_2|$ with $\vec d_1 = \vec a + \vec b$, $\vec d_2 = \vec a - \vec b$.

board_events.latex: (\vec a + \vec b) \times (\vec a - \vec b) = -2(\vec a \times \vec b)

board_events.text: Lagrange gives $|\vec a \times \vec b|$ with no angle computed at all.
Pitfalls and pro-tips
Dot/cross zero-swap: $\vec a \cdot \vec b = 0$ is perpendicular; $\vec a \times \vec b = \vec 0$ is parallel.
Memorise them as opposites and you will never mix them up.
Projection: divide by the magnitude of the vector you project ONTO, not just the dot.
The determinant's $\hat j$ term carries a minus sign, the commonest cross-product slip.
Cross product is NOT commutative: $\vec a \times \vec b = -\,\vec b \times \vec a$.
Pro-tip: the sign of the dot product reads the angle: $+$ acute, $0$ right, $-$ obtuse.
A negative projection must pair with a negative dot product, an instant MCQ check.

segments.text: The dot product immediately hands us two everyday tools: the angle between vectors, and the projection of one onto another.
For the angle, just rearrange the definition to solve for cosine theta.
Cosine theta equals a dot b, divided by the product of the two magnitudes, compute the dot product, divide, take the inverse cosine.
For the projection, we ask how much of a lies along the direction of b.
The scalar projection of a on b is a dot b, divided by the magnitude of b, one clean number.
If you want the projection as a vector, keeping its direction, multiply by b over the magnitude of b squared, the same overlap, now pointing along b.
<whisper>And here is the slip to guard against, you divide by the magnitude of the vector you are projecting onto, not the one being projected.
On the board a casts its shadow onto b, and the length of that shadow is exactly the scalar projection.
Let us collect the working properties of the dot product, the rules you will lean on in every problem.
It is commutative: a dot b equals b dot a, so order never matters for the dot product.
It is distributive over addition: a dot the quantity b plus c splits into a dot b plus a dot c.
A vector dotted with itself gives its magnitude squared, worth memorising, because it turns lengths into dot products.
The perpendicularity test: for non-zero vectors, a dot b equals zero if and only if a is perpendicular to b.
That makes a zero dot product the cleanest possible test for a right angle.
And the sign alone reads the angle for you, positive means acute, zero means a right angle, negative means obtuse.
Armed with these few rules, you can push dot products around just like ordinary algebra.
Now the cross product in symbols, both its geometric definition and the determinant you will actually compute with.
Let n-hat be the unit vector perpendicular to both a and b, with its direction set by the right-hand rule.
Then a cross b equals the magnitude of a, times the magnitude of b, times sine theta, all times n-hat.
If you only need the size, drop the n-hat: the magnitude of a cross b is the magnitude of a, times the magnitude of b, times sine theta.
For computation we use the determinant form, and this is the workhorse of the whole subtopic.
Write a three by three determinant with i-hat, j-hat, k-hat across the top row, the components of a in the second row, and the components of b in the third.
Expanding along the top gives the standard result, the i term, minus the j term, plus the k term, each a little two by two cross-difference.
<whisper>Burn this into memory, the middle term, the j-hat term, carries a minus sign. That single minus is the most common cross-product slip in exams.
The cross product is not just an abstract vector, its magnitude is literally an area, and that makes it a geometry powerhouse.
If a and b are two adjacent sides drawn from a corner, the magnitude of a cross b equals the area of the parallelogram they frame.
So the parallelogram area is simply the magnitude of a cross b.
And a triangle is half a parallelogram, so a triangle with sides a and b from one vertex has area one half the magnitude of a cross b.
The cross product also hands you a direction perpendicular to both vectors at once.
The unit vector perpendicular to both is plus or minus a cross b, divided by its own magnitude.
That plus or minus is genuine: the plane has two opposite normals, and both are perpendicular to it, so both answers are valid.
On the board, a and b span the parallelogram whose area is that magnitude, with the perpendicular standing out of the plane.
Now the working properties of the cross product, ending with the beautiful way it complements the dot product.
It is anti-commutative: a cross b equals minus b cross a, the sign flip we saw from the right-hand rule.
It is distributive over addition, just like the dot product: a cross the quantity b plus c splits into two cross products.
A vector crossed with itself is the zero vector, because the angle is zero and sine zero is zero.
The parallelism test: for non-zero vectors, a cross b equals the zero vector if and only if a is parallel to b.
The basis rule is cyclic: i cross j is k, j cross k is i, k cross i is j, and reversing any pair flips the sign.
Step back and see the harmony: the dot product peaks at zero degrees, while the cross magnitude peaks at ninety degrees.
<excited>On the board those two curves, cosine falling and sine rising, cross exactly at forty five degrees, a perfect complementary pair.
This proof ties the two products together with one elegant identity, Lagrange's identity.
The claim: the square of a dot b, plus the square of the magnitude of a cross b, equals the magnitude of a squared times the magnitude of b squared.
Let theta be the angle between them. Then a dot b is the two magnitudes times cosine theta.
And the magnitude of a cross b is the two magnitudes times sine theta.
Square each and add. Both terms share the factor magnitude of a squared, times magnitude of b squared, leaving cosine squared theta plus sine squared theta.
But cosine squared plus sine squared is one, so the sum is just the magnitude of a squared, times the magnitude of b squared.
The whole proof hinges on that one Pythagorean identity quietly closing the gap.
<whisper>And here is the exam payoff, you can find the magnitude of a cross b directly from a dot b, without ever computing the angle.
Let us run a clean board-level problem that uses the dot product for three things at once.
We have a equals two i-hat plus three j-hat plus k-hat, and b equals i-hat minus two j-hat plus two k-hat, and we want the dot product, the angle, and the projection of a on b.
The dot product first: two times one, plus three times minus two, plus one times two, that is two minus six plus two, which is minus two.
For the angle we need magnitudes. The magnitude of a is root fourteen, and the magnitude of b is root of one plus four plus four, which is three.
So cosine theta is minus two over three root fourteen, and theta is the inverse cosine of that, an obtuse angle, since the cosine is negative.
The projection of a on b is the dot product over the magnitude of b, which is minus two over three.
Notice everything agrees: the negative dot product signals an obtuse angle, and that same negativity shows up in the projection.
So a single dot product quietly fed all three answers, that is the efficiency you want in the exam.
This example is really a test of whether you know which product goes with which condition.
We have a equals lambda i-hat plus two j-hat minus three k-hat, and b equals three i-hat minus j-hat plus two k-hat, and we want lambda for perpendicular, then for parallel.
<whisper>Here is the trap, students reach for the same condition for both. Perpendicular uses the dot product; parallel uses proportional components.
For part one, perpendicular means the dot product is zero.
So three lambda, minus two, minus six equals zero, giving three lambda equals eight, so lambda is eight thirds.
For part two, parallel means the components are proportional: lambda over three equals two over minus one equals minus three over two.
But two over minus one is minus two, while minus three over two is minus one point five, those are not equal.
Since the last two ratios already disagree, no value of lambda can make the vectors parallel. Recognising that saves you a wild goose chase.
This J E E Main level problem puts the cross product to work for both an area and a perpendicular direction.
The two sides from vertex A are a equals three i-hat plus j-hat minus two k-hat, and b equals i-hat minus three j-hat plus four k-hat.

Compute the determinant carefully. The i cofactor is four minus six, minus two; the j cofactor, with its minus sign, is minus the quantity twelve plus two, so minus fourteen; the k cofactor is minus nine minus one, minus ten. So a cross b is minus two i-hat minus fourteen j-hat minus ten k-hat.
Its magnitude is the root of four plus one ninety six plus one hundred, which is root three hundred, or ten root three.
The triangle area is half that magnitude, so five root three square units.
For the perpendicular unit vector, divide the cross product by its magnitude, keeping the plus or minus.
That gives n-hat equals plus or minus one over five root three, times the bracket minus i-hat minus seven j-hat minus five k-hat.
<whisper>And the one thing to watch, the j-hat cofactor carries a minus sign, so minus the quantity twelve plus two is minus fourteen, not plus fourteen.
A J E E Advanced flavoured problem that shows Lagrange's identity earning its keep.

We are told the magnitude of a is five, the magnitude of b is four, and a dot b is ten, and we must find the magnitude of a cross b, then the area of a parallelogram whose diagonals are a plus b and a minus b.
Apply Lagrange: ten squared plus the magnitude of a cross b, squared, equals twenty five times sixteen, which is four hundred.
So the magnitude of a cross b squared is three hundred, giving the magnitude ten root three, and notice we never touched the angle.
Now the area from diagonals. A parallelogram's area is half the magnitude of the cross product of its two diagonals.
Expand a plus b, crossed with a minus b. The self terms vanish, and using b cross a equals minus a cross b, the whole thing is minus two times a cross b.
So the area is half the magnitude of minus two times a cross b, which is just the magnitude of a cross b, namely ten root three.
<excited>Elegant, the answer circles right back to the cross product magnitude, and Lagrange got us there without a single trig calculation.
Let me close the two products with the traps that cost marks, and the pro-tip that saves them.
The biggest one is the zero-condition swap: a dot b equal to zero means perpendicular, while a cross b equal to the zero vector means parallel.
Memorise those two as exact opposites, and you will never mix them up again.
Second, in a projection, always divide by the magnitude of the vector you are projecting onto, do not stop at the bare dot product.
Third, the determinant's j-hat term carries a minus sign; that lone minus is the most common cross-product slip in exams.
Fourth, keep the cross product's order, it is not commutative, so a cross b equals minus b cross a, and swapping matters when direction matters.
And now the pro-tip that pays off instantly: the sign of the dot product reads the angle for you, positive is acute, zero is a right angle, negative is obtuse.
<excited>So a negative projection must pair with a negative dot product; if an option breaks that, eliminate it on sight.

sections.title: The scalar triple product: a volume & related topics

board_events.text: The scalar triple product: a volume
Take three vectors a, b, c from one corner; they frame a slanted box (parallelepiped).
The scalar triple product $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c] = \vec a \cdot (\vec b \times \vec c)$ measures that box's volume.
$\vec b \times \vec c$ gives the base area (as a vector); dotting with a adds the height.
The output is a single number, a scalar, hence 'scalar' triple product.
If the box is flat, the volume is zero, the three vectors are coplanar.

board_events.caption: Three edge vectors a, b, c cage a parallelepiped whose volume is the triple product.

board_events.text: So one number decides both volume AND whether three vectors share a plane.
The vector triple product: back into the plane
Now multiply so the answer is a VECTOR: $\vec a \times (\vec b \times \vec c)$.
$\vec b \times \vec c$ pops OUT of the b-c plane; crossing again with a swings the result BACK into it.
So $\vec a \times (\vec b \times \vec c)$ always lies in the plane of b and c.
It is a blend of b and c, never involving a fresh direction.
The recipe is the 'back cab' rule: $(\vec a \cdot \vec c)\vec b - (\vec a \cdot \vec b)\vec c$.
Brackets are everything: $\vec a \times (\vec b \times \vec c) \neq (\vec a \times \vec b) \times \vec c$.

board_events.caption: b x c stands out of the plane; a x (b x c) lies flat inside the b-c plane.

board_events.text: Three traps with triple products
Scalar vs vector output: $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$ is a number; $\vec a \times (\vec b \times \vec c)$ is a vector.
The vector triple product is NOT associative, brackets cannot be dropped.
Never write $\vec a \times \vec b \times \vec c$ without brackets, it is undefined.
Coplanarity means $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c] = 0$, a flat box, zero volume.
A repeated vector kills the scalar triple product: $[\vec a\ \vec a\ \vec c] = 0$.
Cyclic order is safe; a single swap flips the sign.
Most errors here are misplaced brackets or a forgotten sign.
Scalar triple product: definition and determinant

board_events.latex: [\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c] = \vec a \cdot (\vec b \times \vec c)

board_events.text: In components, it is a single $3\times3$ determinant of the rows:

board_events.latex: [\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c] = \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \\ c_1 & c_2 & c_3 \end{vmatrix}

board_events.text: The sign tells orientation; the absolute value is the volume.
Rows are the three vectors in order, a on top, then b, then c.
One determinant replaces a cross product followed by a dot product.
This is the computational heart of the whole subtopic.
Scalar triple product properties
Cyclic invariance: $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c] = [\vec b\ \vec c\ \vec a] = [\vec c\ \vec a\ \vec b]$.
One swap flips the sign: $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c] = -[\vec b\ \vec a\ \vec c]$.

board_events.latex: \vec a \cdot (\vec b \times \vec c) = (\vec a \times \vec b) \cdot \vec c

board_events.text: Dot and cross can trade places, as long as the cyclic order holds.

board_events.latex: [\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c] = 0 \iff \vec a,\ \vec b,\ \vec c \text{ coplanar}

board_events.text: Any repeated vector gives zero: $[\vec a\ \vec a\ \vec c] = 0$.
These turn ugly expressions into quick sign-and-swap bookkeeping.
Volume applications
Parallelepiped with edges a, b, c from one vertex:
A tetrahedron is one sixth of that same box:
Take the absolute value, a volume is never negative.
For a tetrahedron from four points, use edge vectors from one vertex.

board_events.text: Vector triple product: the back cab rule

board_events.latex: \vec a \times (\vec b \times \vec c) = (\vec a \cdot \vec c)\,\vec b - (\vec a \cdot \vec b)\,\vec c

board_events.text: Memory hook 'back cab': the middle vector b comes first, with a plus sign.
The outer vector a is dotted with each of the inner vectors.

board_events.latex: (\vec a \times \vec b) \times \vec c = (\vec a \cdot \vec c)\,\vec b - (\vec b \cdot \vec c)\,\vec a

board_events.text: Different brackets, different result, the two are generally NOT equal.
The result lies in the plane of the two vectors inside the inner bracket.
Every term is a scalar (a dot product) times a vector, dimensions stay clean.
More on the vector triple product; reciprocal system
Non-associative: $\vec a \times (\vec b \times \vec c) \neq (\vec a \times \vec b) \times \vec c$ in general.
Jacobi identity: the three cyclic vector triple products sum to zero.

segments.text: <curious>We can multiply two vectors two ways. What happens when we bring in a third? The most useful answer measures a volume.
Take three vectors a, b and c, all drawn from a single corner. Together they frame a slanted box, a parallelepiped.
The scalar triple product, written a b c in a box bracket, is a dotted with the quantity b cross c, and it measures the volume of that box.
The logic is lovely: b cross c gives the area of the base, as a vector pointing perpendicular to it, and dotting with a supplies the height.
And the output is a single number, a scalar, which is exactly why it is called the scalar triple product.
Now the powerful special case: if the box is squashed flat, its volume is zero, and that means the three vectors all lie in one plane, they are coplanar.
On the board the three edge vectors a, b and c spring from one corner and cage a solid box whose volume is that triple product.
So a single number does two jobs at once: it gives the volume, and it tells you whether the three vectors share a plane.
The other way to multiply three vectors keeps the answer a vector, and it has a surprising geometry.
This is the vector triple product, a crossed with the quantity b cross c.
Trace the directions: b cross c pops straight out of the plane containing b and c. But then crossing again with a swings the result back down into that very plane.
So here is the key fact, a cross the quantity b cross c always lies in the plane of b and c.
It is a blend, a mixture, of b and c only; it never points off in some fresh third direction.
The exact recipe is the back cab rule: a cross the quantity b cross c equals, a dot c, times b, minus, a dot b, times c.
And brackets are absolutely everything here. a cross the quantity b cross c is not equal to the quantity a cross b, crossed with c, moving the bracket changes the answer.
On the board you can see b cross c standing up out of the plane, while the final vector triple product lies flat inside the b c plane, a combination of the two.
Before the formulas, three traps that triple products set for the unwary.
First, keep the outputs straight: the scalar triple product a b c is a number, while the vector triple product a cross the quantity b cross c is a vector.
Second, and this is the big one, the vector triple product is not associative, you cannot simply drop the brackets.
So never write a cross b cross c with no brackets at all; without them the expression is genuinely undefined.
Third, coplanarity has one crisp test: the scalar triple product equals zero, meaning a flat box of zero volume.
A related fact, if any vector is repeated the scalar triple product collapses to zero, because the box has a degenerate, zero-thickness edge.
For the scalar triple product, cyclic order is safe, but a single swap of two vectors flips the sign, so track your swaps.
Truly, most mistakes in this subtopic are just a misplaced bracket or a forgotten sign, guard those two and you are most of the way home.
Let us make the scalar triple product precise, and then compress it into a single determinant.
By definition, the scalar triple product a b c is a dotted with the quantity b cross c.
But writing it in components reveals something beautiful, it is just one three by three determinant.
Stack the components of a in the top row, b in the middle row, and c in the bottom row, and evaluate that determinant.
The sign of the result tells you the orientation, right handed or left handed, and its absolute value is the volume of the box.
Keep the row order straight, a on top, then b, then c, because swapping rows flips the sign.
The real convenience is that this one determinant replaces a cross product followed by a dot product, two operations folded into one.
This determinant is the computational heart of everything in this subtopic, so it is worth being fast and accurate with it.
The scalar triple product obeys a handful of properties that make it a joy to work with.
First, cyclic invariance: rotating the three vectors in a cycle leaves it unchanged, a b c equals b c a equals c a b.
But a single swap of two vectors flips the sign, so a b c equals minus b a c.
Second, a remarkable interchange, a dotted with b cross c equals a cross b, dotted with c.
In words, the dot and the cross can trade places freely, as long as the cyclic order of the three vectors is preserved.
Third, and most used, the scalar triple product is zero if and only if the three vectors are coplanar, our flat-box test.
And a quick corollary, if any vector is repeated the whole thing is zero, since two equal rows make a determinant vanish.
Together these properties turn frightening-looking expressions into quick sign-and-swap bookkeeping.
The scalar triple product turns directly into volumes, and this is where most exam marks live.
For a parallelepiped, the slanted box with edges a, b and c meeting at a vertex, the volume is simply the modulus of the scalar triple product.
So the parallelepiped volume is the absolute value of a b c.
A tetrahedron, a triangular pyramid, fits exactly six times inside that same box.
So its volume is one sixth of the absolute value of the scalar triple product.
<whisper>Always take the absolute value, the raw triple product can come out negative, but a volume never can.
And when a tetrahedron is given by four points, first build three edge vectors from one common vertex, then feed them in.
On the board the tetrahedron sits inside its parallelepiped, occupying exactly one sixth of the volume.
Now the exact formula for the vector triple product, the single most useful identity in this subtopic.
a cross the quantity b cross c equals, a dot c, times b, minus, a dot b, times c.
The memory hook is back cab: the middle vector b leads, carrying a plus sign, and c follows with a minus.
Notice the pattern, the outer vector a is dotted with each inner vector in turn, producing the two scalar weights.
If instead the bracket sits on the left, the quantity a cross b, then crossed with c, the answer is a dot c times b, minus b dot c times a, a different combination.
So different bracket placements give genuinely different results, the two forms are generally not equal.
In both cases the result lives in the plane of the two vectors inside the inner bracket, exactly as the intuition promised.
And every term is a scalar, a dot product, times a vector, so the dimensions stay perfectly clean throughout.
Two more ideas round out the vector triple product, its non-associativity in identity form, and the elegant reciprocal system.
We saw the vector triple product is not associative, in general a cross the quantity b cross c differs from the quantity a cross b, crossed with c.
But there is a beautiful order in the disorder, called the Jacobi identity.
It says the three cyclic vector triple products, a with b cross c, plus b with c cross a, plus c with a cross b, add up to exactly the zero vector.
Now the reciprocal system. Given three non-coplanar vectors a, b, c forming a basis, let capital V be their scalar triple product.
Define a-prime as b cross c over V, b-prime as c cross a over V, and c-prime as a cross b over V.
These reciprocal vectors have a clean signature, a dot a-prime is one, while a dot b-prime is zero, each original meets its own partner and ignores the others.
<curious>And the reciprocal system exists only when V is non-zero, that is, only when a, b and c are genuinely non-coplanar and form a real basis.
Let us prove that the scalar triple product really is that neat determinant, it follows in three honest steps.
Start from the definition, a b c equals a dotted with the quantity b cross c.
Now write b cross c using its cofactor expansion, the determinant form we proved in the last part.
That gives b cross c as b-two c-three minus b-three c-two along i, minus the next bracket along j, plus the last bracket along k.
Dot this with a, which is a-one i-hat plus a-two j-hat plus a-three k-hat; the dot product simply picks out matching components.
So we get a-one times the i bracket, minus a-two times the j bracket, plus a-three times the k bracket.
But that whole expression is precisely the top-row cofactor expansion of the three by three determinant whose rows are a, b and c.
So the scalar triple product and that determinant are literally the same object, written two ways.
This proof explains the two friendliest properties of the scalar triple product using one fact about determinants.
The fact is simple: swapping any two rows of a determinant flips its sign.
A cyclic rotation of the three rows is really two swaps back to back, and two sign flips cancel, so the value returns unchanged.
That is exactly the cyclic property, a b c equals b c a equals c a b.
And a single swap, being just one flip, gives a b c equals minus b a c, as claimed.

Now the dot-cross interchange. Compute a dotted with b cross c and it equals the determinant with rows a, b, c. Compute a cross b, dotted with c, and by cyclic rotation it equals the very same determinant.
So a dotted with b cross c equals a cross b, dotted with c.
The deep reason is geometric, both expressions are just two ways of measuring the identical box, so they cannot help but agree.
The back cab rule is worth verifying, so you trust it under pressure. We will check it on a clean basis example, and note how the full proof extends.
The identity to confirm is a cross the quantity b cross c equals, a dot c times b, minus a dot b times c.
Take a simple case: a is i-hat, b is i-hat, and c is j-hat.
First the inner cross product, b cross c is i-hat cross j-hat, which is k-hat.
Then the outer cross, a cross that, is i-hat cross k-hat, and by the cyclic rules that is minus j-hat.
Now the right-hand side: a dot c is i-hat dot j-hat, which is zero; a dot b is i-hat dot i-hat, which is one. So we get zero times b, minus one times c, which is minus j-hat.
Both sides land on minus j-hat, so the identity checks out on this case.
The full proof simply repeats this on each basis combination and then extends to all vectors by linearity, since both sides are linear in a, b and c.

sections.title: Example: box product and volume & related topics

board_events.text: Example: box product and volume
$\vec a = \hat i + 2\hat j + 3\hat k$, $\vec b = 2\hat i - \hat j + \hat k$, $\vec c = 3\hat i + \hat j - \hat k$. Find the parallelepiped volume.
Expand along the top row with the alternating signs.
Non-zero, so the three vectors are non-coplanar (a genuine solid box).
Example: the coplanarity trap
Find $\lambda$ so that $\vec a = \hat i + \hat j + \hat k$, $\vec b = 2\hat i + 3\hat j + 2\hat k$, $\vec c = \hat i + \lambda\hat j + 3\hat k$ are coplanar.
Coplanarity requires the scalar triple product to vanish:
The $\lambda$ terms cancel, leaving $2 = 0$, which is impossible.
So NO value of $\lambda$ makes them coplanar, the honest answer is 'no solution'.
Example: tetrahedron volume from four points
Vertices $P(1,1,1)$, $Q(2,1,3)$, $R(3,2,1)$, $S(1,3,2)$. Find the tetrahedron's volume.
Build three edge vectors from P:

board_events.latex: \vec{PQ} = \hat i + 2\hat k,\quad \vec{PR} = 2\hat i + \hat j,\quad \vec{PS} = 2\hat j + \hat k

board_events.text: All three edges must start from the SAME vertex P.
Example: vector triple product with back cab
$\vec a = \hat i + \hat j$, $\vec b = \hat j + \hat k$, $\vec c = \hat i + \hat k$. Find $\vec a \times (\vec b \times \vec c)$.
Use the back cab rule, avoid computing the inner cross first.

board_events.latex: \vec a \times (\vec b \times \vec c) = (\vec a \cdot \vec c)\vec b - (\vec a \cdot \vec b)\vec c
= 1(\hat j + \hat k) - 1(\hat i + \hat k) = -\hat i + \hat j

board_events.text: Check: the result has no component along the normal of the b-c plane.
back cab beats brute force, two dot products instead of two cross products.
Pitfalls and pro-tips
Coplanarity test is $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c] = 0$; a non-zero constant means 'no solution'.
If $\lambda$ cancels and leaves a false equation, answer honestly: no solution.
Vector triple product: NEVER drop the brackets, and the middle vector leads (back cab).
Tetrahedron volume is $\tfrac{1}{6}$ of the box; the parallelepiped is the full $|[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]|$.
Take the absolute value for any volume, a raw triple product may be negative.
Track sign on row swaps; cyclic order keeps the value, one swap flips it.
Pro-tip: use back cab (two dot products) instead of two cross products, every time.
Where does a point live in 3D?
Three mutually perpendicular axes x, y, z meet at the origin O; a point is the triple (x, y, z).
Axes in pairs give three planes: xy-plane $(z=0)$, yz-plane $(x=0)$, zx-plane $(y=0)$.
Right-handed system: curl fingers x toward y, thumb points +z.
The three planes cut space into eight octants; the first has all coordinates positive.

board_events.text: Projection onto xy-plane is $(x, y, 0)$; onto the x-axis it is $(x, 0, 0)$.
Distance from x-axis $=\sqrt{y^2+z^2}$; distance from xy-plane $=|z|$.
Centroid, volume, area, and collinearity
The centroid is the balance point: equal masses at the vertices balance at G.
For a tetrahedron the centroid divides the vertex sum by 4.
Collinear $\iff$ direction ratios proportional $\iff$ area $=0$.
Centroid cuts each median $2:1$ from the vertex.
Find the distance between $A(1,-2,3)$ and $B(4,2,-1)$
Take coordinate differences $B-A$ inside each bracket.
$2-(-2)=4$ — expanding the double negative saves a whole term.
The sign of each difference disappears on squaring, so P and Q are interchangeable.
Divide $A(2,-1,4)$ and $B(4,3,2)$ internally in $1:3$
Set $m:n=1:3$; weight $m=1$ rides far endpoint $B$, $n=3$ rides near $A$.
$n=3$ is larger, so the point leans toward $A$ — the quick check.
A $1:3$ split from A landing nearer A confirms the weights were placed correctly.
In what ratio does the yz-plane divide $A(2,4,5)$–$B(3,5,-4)$?
The yz-plane is $x=0$; let the ratio be $k:1$ from A.
Negative $k$ signals external division — the plane cuts outside the segment.
The sign carried the geometric meaning — a recurring JEE Main theme.
Both A and B have positive $x$, so they lie on the same side — the cut must be external.
Volume of the tetrahedron $A(1,1,1),B(3,2,1),C(2,4,2),D(1,2,5)$
Take the three edge vectors from vertex A.
The modulus is essential — a volume can never be negative.
You may use edges from any vertex — the volume is the same, a handy cross-check.

segments.text: Let us compute an actual volume with the determinant, a bread-and-butter J E E Main problem.

We have a equals i-hat plus two j-hat plus three k-hat, b equals two i-hat minus j-hat plus k-hat, and c equals three i-hat plus j-hat minus k-hat, and we want the volume of the parallelepiped they span.
Set up the determinant with a, b and c as its three rows.
Expand along the top row, remembering the alternating plus, minus, plus signs.
The first minor is one minus one; the second, with its minus sign in front, is minus two minus three; the third is two plus three.
That is one times zero, minus two times minus five, plus three times five, which is zero plus ten plus fifteen, equal to twenty five.
The volume is the absolute value, so twenty five cubic units.
And since the triple product is non-zero, the three vectors are non-coplanar, they really do cage a solid box, not a flat sheet.
This example looks routine but hides a genuine trap, and reading the algebra honestly is the whole point.
We must find lambda so that a equals i-hat plus j-hat plus k-hat, b equals two i-hat plus three j-hat plus two k-hat, and c equals i-hat plus lambda j-hat plus three k-hat are coplanar.
Coplanarity requires the scalar triple product to vanish, so we set the determinant equal to zero.
Write the determinant with the three vectors as rows and expand along the top.
The first term is one times nine minus two lambda; the second, with its minus, is minus the quantity six minus two; the third is two lambda minus three.
Now watch carefully as we simplify: nine minus two lambda, minus four, plus two lambda, minus three. The two-lambda terms cancel, and the constants give two.
<curious>So the equation collapses to two equals zero, which is simply impossible, and notice the lambda vanished entirely.
Therefore no value of lambda can make these vectors coplanar; the honest, correct answer is that there is no solution. A student who forces a number here has fallen straight into the trap.
A J E E Main favourite, finding the volume of a tetrahedron given its four corner points.
The vertices are P at one, one, one; Q at two, one, three; R at three, two, one; and S at one, three, two.
The key first move is to build three edge vectors, all starting from the same vertex, say P.
P Q is Q minus P, which is i-hat plus two k-hat; P R is two i-hat plus j-hat; and P S is two j-hat plus k-hat.
Now form the scalar triple product of these three edges as a determinant.
Expanding along the top row: one times the minor one, minus zero, plus two times the minor four, giving one plus eight, which is nine.
The tetrahedron volume is one sixth of the absolute value, so one sixth of nine, which is three halves.
<whisper>The one non-negotiable step, all three edge vectors must start from the same vertex; mix your starting points and the volume is meaningless.
Finally, let us see the back cab rule save real time on a vector triple product.
We have a equals i-hat plus j-hat, b equals j-hat plus k-hat, and c equals i-hat plus k-hat, and we want a cross the quantity b cross c.
The lazy but wrong instinct is to compute the inner cross product first; the smart move is to apply the back cab rule directly.
We only need two dot products: a dot c is one, and a dot b is one.
The rule says the answer is, a dot c times b, minus a dot b times c.
So that is one times the quantity j-hat plus k-hat, minus one times the quantity i-hat plus k-hat, and the k-hats cancel, leaving minus i-hat plus j-hat.
A nice consistency check, the result has no component sticking out along the normal to the b c plane, exactly as the geometry demanded.
<excited>See the economy, back cab needed just two dot products, where brute force would have cost two full cross products.
Let me close the final subtopic, and the chapter, with the traps that bite and the tricks that save.
The coplanarity test is that the scalar triple product equals zero; if instead it reduces to a non-zero constant, that means no solution exists.
So if lambda cancels and you are left with a false equation like two equals zero, do not panic and do not invent a value, answer honestly that there is no solution.
For the vector triple product, never ever drop the brackets, and remember the middle vector leads in back cab, with a plus sign.
Keep the two volumes distinct, a tetrahedron is one sixth of the box, while the parallelepiped is the full absolute value of the triple product.
Always take the absolute value for a volume, because the raw scalar triple product can come out negative depending on orientation.
And track your signs on row swaps, cyclic order preserves the value, but each single swap flips the sign.
<excited>The headline pro-tip for the whole subtopic, reach for back cab, two cheap dot products, rather than grinding out two full cross products, every single time.
<curious>Let's start with the most basic question of the whole chapter</curious> — how do we pin down exactly where a point sits in three dimensional space?
Picture the corner of a room: three edges meet there at right angles. Call them the x, y and z axes, and the corner the origin. Any point is reached by walking x, then y, then z steps.
Taken in pairs, the axes define three flat walls. The xy-plane is where z equals zero, the yz-plane where x equals zero, and the zx-plane where y equals zero.
We always use the right handed system. Curl the fingers of your right hand from the positive x axis toward positive y, and your thumb points along positive z. Every formula assumes this.

These three planes slice all of space into eight compartments called octants — the three dimensional cousins of the four quadrants. The first octant is the friendly one where all three coordinates are positive.
Here is a point P and its shadow. Drop P straight down onto the floor and it lands at the point with the same x and y but height zero — that is its projection onto the xy plane.
Projecting onto a plane flattens one coordinate to zero. Projecting onto an axis keeps only one coordinate — onto the x axis, the point lands at x, zero, zero.

These projections make distances easy. The distance of a point from the x axis is root y squared plus z squared — a two coordinate Pythagoras. But the distance from the xy plane is just the size of z. Read axis as two coordinates, plane as one.
The averaging idea extends naturally from two points to three or four, and it quietly powers tests for area, volume and whether points lie on a line.
Physically the centroid is the balance point. Place equal masses at the vertices of a triangle and they balance exactly at the centroid — a plain, unweighted average of the vertices.
For a triangle, the centroid is the average of the three vertices — divide each coordinate sum by three.
For a tetrahedron, the same idea gives the balance point as one quarter of the vertex sum — you simply divide by four instead of three.
The volume of a tetrahedron is one sixth of the scalar triple product of its three edge vectors from one vertex. The triple product is the volume of the slanted box built on those edges.
The area of a triangle is half the magnitude of the cross product of two edge vectors.
