isliye koi bhi lambda in vectors ko coplanar nahin bana sakta; imandaar, sahi jawab hai ki koi solution nahin hai. jo student yahaan zabardasti ek number nikaalta hai wo seedha trap mein gir gaya.
ek J E E Main favourite, chaar corner points diye hone par tetrahedron ka volume nikaalna.
Vertices hain P at one, one, one; Q at two, one, three; R at three, two, one; aur S at one, three, two.
Key pehla move hai teen edge vectors banana, sab ek hi vertex se shuru, maan lo P se.
P Q hai Q minus P, jo i-hat plus two k-hat hai; P R hai two i-hat plus j-hat; aur P S hai two j-hat plus k-hat.
ab in teenon edges ka scalar triple product ek determinant ke roop mein banao.
Top row ke along expand karke: one times the minor one, minus zero, plus two times the minor four, yaani one plus eight, jo nine hai.
Tetrahedron volume absolute value ka one sixth hai, to nine ka one sixth, jo three halves hai.
ek non-negotiable step, teenon edge vectors ek hi vertex se shuru hone chahiye; starting points mix kiye to volume meaningless hai.
aakhir mein, dekhte hain back cab rule ek vector triple product par asli time kaise bachati hai.
hamare paas a equals i-hat plus j-hat, b equals j-hat plus k-hat, aur c equals i-hat plus k-hat, aur chahiye a cross the quantity b cross c.
Lazy par ghalat instinct hai pehle inner cross product compute karna; smart move hai back cab rule seedha apply karna.
humein sirf do dot products chahiye: a dot c hai one, aur a dot b hai one.
Rule kahati hai answer hai, a dot c times b, minus a dot b times c.
to wo hai one times the quantity j-hat plus k-hat, minus one times the quantity i-hat plus k-hat, aur k-hats cancel ho jaate hain, bachta hai minus i-hat plus j-hat.
ek acchā consistency check, result kā koī component b c plane ke normal ke along bāhar nahīṅ nikalta, ṭhīk jaisā geometry ne māngā.
Economy dekho, back cab ko sirf do dot products chahiye the, jahan brute force ko do poore cross products lagte.
aakhiri subtopic, aur chapter, ko un traps ke saath close karte hain jo kaat te hain aur un tricks ke saath jo bachati hain.
Coplanarity test ye hai ki scalar triple product zero ke equal ho; agar bajay iske ye ek non-zero constant mein reduce ho, to matlab koi solution exist nahi karta.
to agar lambda cancel ho jaaye aur aapke paas ek false equation bache jaise two equals zero, ghabraao mat aur koi value mat banao, imaandari se jawab do ki koi solution nahi hai.
Vector triple product ke liye, brackets kabhi mat drop karo, aur yaad rakho back cab mein middle vector aage rehta hai, plus sign ke saath.
donon volumes alag rakho, tetrahedron box ka one sixth hai, jabki parallelepiped triple product ka poora absolute value hai.
kisi bhi volume ke liye hamesha absolute value lo, kyunki raw scalar triple product orientation ke hisaab se negative aa sakta hai.
aur row swaps par apne signs track karo, cyclic order value preserve karta hai, par har single swap sign flip karta hai.
poore subtopic ke liye headline pro-tip, back cab uthao, do saste dot products, bajay do poore cross products peesne ke, har baar.
chaliye poore chapter ke sabse basic sawaal se shuru karte hain — three dimensional space mein kisi point ki exact jagah hum kaise batayen?

ek kamre ka corner sochiye: vahaan teen edges right angle par milti hain. inhen hum x, y aur z axis kahte hain, aur us corner ko origin. kisi bhi point tak pahunchne ke liye x, phir y, phir z steps chalte hain.
jodiyon mein lene par ye axes teen flat walls banate hain. xy-plane vahaan hai jahan z zero hai, yz-plane jahan x zero hai, aur zx-plane jahan y zero hai.

ham hamesha right handed system use karte hain. apne right hand ki fingers ko positive x axis se positive y ki taraf modiye, thumb positive z ki direction mein point karega. har formula yahi maanta hai.

ye teen planes poore space ko aath compartments mein kaat te hain, jinhen octants kahte hain — ye quadrants ke three dimensional cousins hain. pehla octant vo friendly wala hai jahan teenon coordinates positive hote hain.
yahaan ek point P hai aur uski shadow. P ko seedhe neeche floor par giraaiye to wo usi x aur y par, par height zero ke saath land karta hai — yahi uska xy plane par projection hai.
kisi plane par project karne se ek coordinate zero ho jata hai. kisi axis par project karne se sirf ek coordinate bachta hai — x axis par point x, zero, zero par land karta hai.

in projections se distances aasan ho jaati hain. kisi point ki x axis se distance hai root y squared plus z squared — ek two coordinate Pythagoras. par xy plane se distance sirf z ka size hai. axis ko two coordinate padhiye, plane ko one.
Averaging wala idea do points se teen ya chaar points tak naturally badhta hai, aur ye chupchaap area, volume aur points ke ek line par hone ke tests ko chalata hai.
Physically centroid balance point hai. Ek triangle ke vertices par equal masses rakhiye to wo theek centroid par balance karti hain — vertices ka ek plain, bina weight wala average.
ek triangle ke liye centroid teenon vertices ka average hai — har coordinate ke sum ko teen se divide kijiye.
ek tetrahedron ke liye, wahi idea balance point ko vertex sum ka one quarter deta hai — bas teen ki jagah chaar se divide kijiye.
ek tetrahedron ka volume uske ek vertex se teen edge vectors ke scalar triple product ka one sixth hai. triple product un edges par bane slanted box ka volume hai.
ek triangle ka area do edge vectors ke cross product ke magnitude ka half hai.
vo area ek collinearity test bhi hai. teen points theek tab collinear hain jab unka banaya triangle zero area ka ho — yaani jab ek point se baakiyon tak direction ratios proportional hon.
ek saaf fact yaad rakhiye: centroid har median par hota hai aur use two to one ratio mein kaatata hai, vertex se opposite side ke midpoint tak naapte hue.
chaliye ek saaf distance problem karte hain. humein A, one, minus two, three, aur B, four, two, minus one ke beech distance chahiye.
ham har bracket mein coordinates ka difference lete hain, B minus A. sabse tricky bracket y wala hai, jahan ham two minus negative two nikalte hain.
Substitute karne par: root jismein four minus one squared, plus two minus negative two squared, plus negative one minus three squared.
har bracket teen, chaar aur minus four mein simplify hota hai. dhyaan dijiye double negative ne beech wale term mein saaf chaar diya.
Square karke jodne par nau plus solah plus solah milta hai, yaani iktaalis. To distance hai root iktaalis units.
yahaan sabse common galti hai two minus two equals zero likh dena, jisse chupke se ek term kho jaata hai. hamesha double negative ko explicitly expand kijiye.
aur kyonki har difference square hota hai, uska sign gayab ho jata hai — to sach mein fark nahi padta aapne kise A kaha aur kise B.
ab ek section formula problem. hum A, two, minus one, four, aur B, four, three, two ke join ko one to three ratio mein internally baant te hain.
to m ek hai aur n teen. yaad rakhiye, m far endpoint B par baithta hai, aur n near endpoint A par. hum har coordinate mein weighted average lagate hain.
x coordinate hai one times four plus three times two, sab chaar par — yaani ten over four.
y coordinate hai one times three plus three times minus one, chaar par — numerator zero hai.
aur z coordinate hai one times two plus three times four, chaar par — fourteen over four.
Simplify karne par, dividing point hai five halves, zero, seven halves.
yahaan geometric sanity check hai. kyonki n, near endpoint A par ka weight, bada hai, answer ko A ki taraf jhukna chahiye — aur yahi hota hai, ye B ke muqable A ke kareeb baithta hai.
A se naapa gaya one to three split A ke kareeb land karna confirm karta hai ki weights sahi endpoints par baithe the. Wo ek nazar zyadaatar weight swapping ki galtiyan pakad leti hai.
is problem mein ek sign ka sabak chhupa hai. y z plane, A, two, four, five aur B, three, five, minus four ko jodne wale segment ko kis ratio mein baantta hai?
y z plane bas wo set hai jahan x zero hai. maan lijiye unknown ratio, A se napa hua, k to one hai. humein sirf dividing point ka x coordinate chahiye.
Section formula se, x coordinate hai k times three plus one times two, over k plus one — yaani three k plus two over k plus one.
us x coordinate ko zero rakhiye, kyunki point plane par hai. tab three k plus two equals zero, jo k ko minus two thirds deta hai.

vo negative value galti nahin hai — ye geometry bol rahi hai. negative k external division ka sanket deta hai: plane line ko segment ke baahar milta hai, use two to three ratio mein externally baantte hue.
to sign ne poora geometric meaning dhoya, aur ek calculation ne ratio aur uska type dono diye. ye idea J E E Main mein baar-baar lautata hai.

Geometrically ye sahi baithta hai: A aur B dono ka x positive hai, to wo y z plane ke ek hi side par hain. plane ek hi side ke do points ke beech se nahi guzhar sakta, to wo unki line ko sirf ek extension par mil sakta hai — externally.
Chaliye scalar triple product se ek tetrahedron ka volume nikalte hain. Vertices A, B, C aur D hain, jaisa dikhaya gaya hai.
pehle hum vertex A se shuru hone wale teen edge vectors banate hain — yaani A ko B, C aur D mein se ghataate hain.
ye dete hain A B barabar two, one, zero; A C barabar one, three, one; aur A D barabar zero, one, four.
ab A C ko A D ke saath cross kijiye. determinant expand karne par eleven, minus four, one milta hai.
use A B ke saath dot kijiye: two times eleven, plus one times minus four, plus zero — yaani baais minus four, barabar athaarah.
Volume atharah ke size ka one sixth hai, yaani teen cubic units.
Absolute value zaroori hai. negative triple product ka matlab sirf itna hai ki edges ek left handed set banate hain; volume khud kabhi negative nahi ho sakta.
aur aap edges kisi bhi vertex se le sakte hain; volume same aata hai. ye ek handy cross check hai agar aapki pehli computation kabhi galat lage.

sections.title: Foundations: pitfalls and pro-tips & related topics

board_events.text: Where students lose foundation marks
Weight $m$ rides the FAR endpoint $x_2$; swapping puts the point on the wrong side.
A negative division ratio is not an error — it means external division.
Distance is the root of the sum of squares, never $|\Delta x|+|\Delta y|+|\Delta z|$.
The $AB+BC=AC$ collinearity test needs correct ordering; else use direction ratios.
Axis drops one coordinate; plane keeps only one.
Keep the modulus on area and volume; a centroid must lie inside the triangle.
Which way does a line point?
A line makes angles $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ with the x, y, z axes.
Think of a fixed total strength of 1 spent across the three axes.

board_events.text: Direction cosines are the components of the unit vector along the line.
Equally inclined line: $l=m=n=\pm\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$.
Direction ratios: proportional to the cosines
Coordinate differences give a natural step, e.g. $(3,6,8)$ for a line through two points.
Any triple proportional to the direction cosines is a set of direction ratios.
Direction ratios are never unique; direction cosines are unique up to $\pm$.
Reverse the line and every sign flips: $(l,m,n)\to(-l,-m,-n)$.
The zero triple $(0,0,0)$ has no direction and is meaningless as ratios.
A point and a direction fix a line
A line carries two independent pieces: where it is, and which way it goes.
The same direction ratios describe infinitely many parallel lines.

$\cos\gamma=-\tfrac12$ is equally valid — write BOTH answers.

$A(3,-1,2),B(1,3,4),C(5,k,0)$ collinear — find $k$ and the DCs

Direction-cosine traps to dodge

Never forget the $\pm$ — an undirected line has two direction-cosine sets.
The angle with an axis and with the perpendicular plane are complementary, not equal.
Standardise a Cartesian equation before reading off direction ratios.
$\lambda$ is a length only with a unit direction vector.
After every DC answer, square them and confirm the sum is 1.
How do two lines cross, and how close do they come?
Lines that neither meet nor run parallel are called skew lines.
The angle between two lines depends only on their directions, never on position.
Wrap the numerator in $|\cdot|$ — we always report the acute angle.
Think of the dot product as a sameness meter.

segments.text: Before we move on, let's lock in the handful of slips that cost the easiest marks in this whole section.
First, the section formula weights. The weight m multiplies the far endpoint, and n the near one. Swapping them places the point on the wrong side entirely.
Second, do not panic at a negative ratio. A negative answer for the ratio is not a mistake; it simply tells you the cut lies outside the segment.
Third, distance is always the root of a sum of squared differences — never the sum of the magnitudes of the differences. Neither the squaring nor the rooting may be skipped.

Fourth, the additive distance test for collinearity only works when the middle point genuinely sits between the other two. When the order is unknown, switch to proportional direction ratios, which never depend on ordering.

Fifth, never confuse distance from an axis with distance from a plane. Distance from an axis drops the shared coordinate and keeps two under the root; distance from a plane keeps only the single zeroed coordinate.

Finally, area and volume are magnitudes, so the modulus is non negotiable. And a quick sanity check — a centroid must lie strictly inside its triangle, so a centroid landing beyond a vertex signals an arithmetic slip.
<curious>Here is the single most important question we can ask about a line in space</curious> — not where it is, but which way it points.
In two dimensions one angle was enough. But in space, which way needs to be pinned down against all three axes at once, so we measure the angles alpha, beta and gamma with the x, y and z axes.
Rather than carry three angles, we carry their cosines: l is cos alpha, m is cos beta, n is cos gamma. These three numbers are the direction cosines of the line.
Think of direction cosines like splitting a budget. A direction has a fixed total strength of one, and it must spend that strength across the three axes.
The hidden rule that makes it a budget is the master identity: l squared plus m squared plus n squared equals one. The squares always add to exactly one.

Here is the picture. Take a point P on the line at distance r from the origin; its shadow on each axis is r times the corresponding cosine. So the direction cosines are the fractions of the length spent along each axis.
In one sentence worth memorising: the direction cosines are the components of the unit vector pointing along the line. A single unit step moves you l to the right, m forward and n upward.

<whisper>One value worth memorising outright</whisper> — a line equally inclined to all three axes has each direction cosine equal to plus or minus one over root three, because three l squared must equal one.
Nobody wants to compute three cosines from scratch every time. Direction ratios are the shortcut, and they are far easier to read off.
If a line passes through the points one, two, three and four, eight, eleven, the natural step along it is three, six, eight — just the coordinate differences.

Those numbers are not the direction cosines — their squares do not sum to one — but they are proportional to them. Any triple proportional to the direction cosines is a set of direction ratios. Think of it like a recipe given as a ratio.

To get the unique unit version, the direction cosines, you divide each ratio by the length root a squared plus b squared plus c squared. The single plus or minus reflects the two directions of the line.

An important asymmetry: direction ratios are never unique — two, three, minus one and four, six, minus two describe the same line. Only the direction cosines are unique, up to that single plus or minus.
Direction cosines belong to a directed line. Reverse the arrow and every sign flips together, which is exactly why the plus or minus keeps appearing.
One boundary case: the zero triple, zero, zero, zero, points nowhere and is meaningless as direction ratios. A valid set is never all zero.
Once you know a single point on a line and its direction, the line is completely determined — like knowing a train's starting station and the exact bearing of the track.

It pays to see how cleanly this separates two ideas. A line carries two completely independent pieces of information: where it is, given by any one point, and which way it goes, given by its direction.
The vector equation captures both. Position vector a supplies the where, direction b supplies the which way, and the parameter lambda slides you up and down the track.

Direction cosines and ratios capture only the which way, which is exactly why the same direction ratios describe infinitely many parallel lines scattered across space. To name one specific line, you must marry a direction to a point.

Eliminating lambda gives the Cartesian symmetric form: x minus x one over a, equals y minus y one over b, equals z minus z one over c. The denominators are the direction ratios; the constants are the point.
For a line through two points, the direction ratios are just the coordinate differences, so the two point form places those differences in the denominators.
Here is the geometry: start at the point a, and step any distance along the direction b. Every point on the line is reached for some value of lambda.

One caution baked into the form: lambda equals true distance from the base point only when b is a unit vector — that is, when its components are the direction cosines themselves. With arbitrary direction ratios, lambda is just a parameter, not a length.
A clean board level problem. A line has direction ratios two, minus three, six. Find its direction cosines, and write the equations of the line through one, four, minus two parallel to it.
First the length of the direction ratio triple: root of four plus nine plus thirty six, which is root forty nine, equal to seven.
Dividing each ratio by seven gives the direction cosines: two sevenths, minus three sevenths, six sevenths.
Always run the one second check: four over forty nine plus nine over forty nine plus thirty six over forty nine equals one. The normalisation is confirmed.
The vector equation places the point one, four, minus two as a, and the direction ratios two, minus three, six as b.
And the Cartesian equation simply reuses the direction ratios as denominators and the point's coordinates, with signs flipped, as the constants.
Notice the lesson: the equation of a line is, in effect, just its direction and one point written side by side.
This is a classic speed trap. A line makes sixty degrees with the x axis and forty five degrees with the y axis. What angle does it make with the z axis?
We do not need to find all the direction cosines. We can use the identity that the sum of the squared cosines of the three angles equals one, directly.
Substituting the two known angles: cos squared sixty plus cos squared forty five plus cos squared gamma equals one.
Cos squared sixty is one quarter and cos squared forty five is one half. So cos squared gamma is one quarter.
Taking the square root gives cos gamma equal to plus or minus one half. So gamma is sixty degrees or one hundred twenty degrees — both are valid.

<whisper>Here is the trap</whisper> — most students stop at sixty degrees and lose the mark. Because cos gamma equals minus one half is equally valid, the line may dip below the plane and make one hundred twenty degrees. The moment you see cos squared alone, write two answers.
So the speed move is simple: the instant a problem hands you cos squared gamma alone, reach for the plus or minus reflex and report both angles.
This links two skills. The points A, B and C are collinear. Find the unknown k, and then the direction cosines of the line.
Form the two direction ratio vectors from A. A B is minus two, four, two, and A C is two, k plus one, minus two.
Collinearity means these are proportional. The first and third ratios both equal minus one, which is consistent.
From the middle ratio, k plus one over four equals minus one, so k plus one is minus four, giving k equal to minus five.
Now use A B, which is minus two, four, two, with magnitude root twenty four, equal to two root six.
Dividing each component by two root six and simplifying gives direction cosines minus one over root six, two over root six, one over root six.

The cross check is automatic: one sixth plus four sixths plus one sixth equals one. Note that any scalar multiple would have served as direction ratios; we normalised only at the very last step — the disciplined order that guards against reporting ratios where cosines were asked.
An advanced problem. The direction cosines of two lines satisfy a linear relation, three l plus m plus five n equals zero, and a quadratic relation. Find the acute angle between the two lines.
From the linear relation, solve for m: m equals minus the quantity three l plus five n. Then substitute this into the quadratic.
After substituting and simplifying, the quadratic collapses to l squared plus three l n plus two n squared equals zero, which factors as l plus n times l plus two n.
The first factor gives l equals minus n. Back substituting into the linear relation, the first line has direction ratios proportional to one, two, minus one.
The second factor gives l equals minus two n, and the second line has direction ratios proportional to two, minus one, minus one. Both vectors have magnitude root six.
The cosine of the angle is the dot product over the product of magnitudes: two minus two plus one, over six, which is one sixth. So theta is the inverse cosine of one sixth, about eighty degrees.

Two takeaways: one linear plus one quadratic relation generically carves out two directions, which is why the question refers to two lines. And we never needed the actual direction cosines, because the angle formula is scale free.
Let's close this subtopic by locking in the traps that examiners set again and again around direction cosines and line equations.
First, the most common blunder — writing direction ratios as the answer without dividing by their length. Whenever cosines are asked, always finish with the normalisation step.
Second, never forget the plus or minus. An undirected line has two opposite direction cosine sets, and problems that reach cos squared of an angle usually have two valid angle answers.
Third, do not confuse the angle a line makes with an axis and the angle it makes with the plane perpendicular to that axis. They are complementary, not equal.

Fourth, an equation written with a coefficient on x, y or z, or with a numerator like three minus y, hides its true direction ratios. Spend three seconds forcing it into standard form before reading the ratios — that skipped step is the cheapest mark on the page.
Fifth, do not treat the parameter lambda as a distance. Lambda is a true length only when the direction vector is a unit vector — that is, when you used direction cosines rather than raw ratios.
And a one second habit that saves whole problems: after every direction cosine answer, square the three values and confirm the sum is one. If it is not, you forgot to normalise.

<curious>Picture two metro tunnels bored deep under a city — they never meet and they are not parallel</curious>. Two natural questions arise: at what angle do they cross, and what is the thinnest wall of earth between them?
Lines in space that neither meet nor run parallel, like these tunnels, are called skew lines, and they are the heart of this subtopic.

Take the angle first. The liberating idea is that the angle between two lines depends only on their directions, never on where they sit. So we slide both directions to a common point and measure between the arrows.
That is exactly the dot product. The cosine of the angle is the dot product of the two direction vectors, divided by the product of their magnitudes.

There is one subtlety. A line points two opposite ways, so the dot product might come out negative, suggesting an obtuse angle. By convention we report the acute angle, so we wrap the numerator in a modulus.

Think of the dot product as a sameness meter. When two directions align it is large and positive; when perpendicular it is exactly zero; when they oppose it is large and negative. Strip the sign and you have the cosine of the sharp angle.
This instantly hands you two free tests: the lines are perpendicular when the dot product is zero, and parallel when the direction ratios are proportional.
Now the shortest distance. Picture the thinnest wall between the tunnels. The shortest segment connecting two skew lines is special: it is perpendicular to both lines at once.

Think of two pencils held crookedly in the air. The shortest gap between them is bridged by a third tiny stick that meets both pencils at right angles. Which way must that stick point? Perpendicular to both directions at once.
And the cross product of the two directions is built to be exactly that common perpendicular. Here it is, bridging the two lines. The gap d is measured only along this direction.

So we take any vector joining the two lines, the vector a two minus a one between their reference points, and measure only its component along that common perpendicular direction. Everything else runs along the tunnels and does not count toward the gap.
That projection gives the shortest distance: the scalar triple product of the joining vector with the cross product, divided by the size of that cross product.

There is a lovely reading of this. The scalar triple product is the volume of the slanted box built on those three vectors. Divide that volume by the area of its base, the size of the cross product, and you get its height — and the height is the perpendicular gap. Distance is volume per unit base area.
So the whole computation is three vector operations chained together: a cross product to find the common perpendicular, a dot product to project the joining vector, and a magnitude to finish.

chunk_timeline.text: Before we move on, let's lock in the handful of slips that cost the easiest marks in this whole section.
First, the section formula weights. The weight m multiplies the far endpoint, and n the near one. Swapping them places the point on the wrong side entirely.
Second, do not panic at a negative ratio. A negative answer for the ratio is not a mistake; it simply tells you the cut lies outside the segment.
Third, distance is always the root of a sum of squared differences — never the sum of the magnitudes of the differences. Neither the squaring nor the rooting may be skipped.

Fourth, the additive distance test for collinearity only works when the middle point genuinely sits between the other two. When the order is unknown, switch to proportional direction ratios, which never depend on ordering.

Fifth, never confuse distance from an axis with distance from a plane. Distance from an axis drops the shared coordinate and keeps two under the root; distance from a plane keeps only the single zeroed coordinate.

Finally, area and volume are magnitudes, so the modulus is non negotiable. And a quick sanity check — a centroid must lie strictly inside its triangle, so a centroid landing beyond a vertex signals an arithmetic slip.
<curious>Here is the single most important question we can ask about a line in space</curious> — not where it is, but which way it points.
In two dimensions one angle was enough. But in space, which way needs to be pinned down against all three axes at once, so we measure the angles alpha, beta and gamma with the x, y and z axes.
Rather than carry three angles, we carry their cosines: l is cos alpha, m is cos beta, n is cos gamma. These three numbers are the direction cosines of the line.
Think of direction cosines like splitting a budget. A direction has a fixed total strength of one, and it must spend that strength across the three axes.
The hidden rule that makes it a budget is the master identity: l squared plus m squared plus n squared equals one. The squares always add to exactly one.

Here is the picture. Take a point P on the line at distance r from the origin; its shadow on each axis is r times the corresponding cosine. So the direction cosines are the fractions of the length spent along each axis.
In one sentence worth memorising: the direction cosines are the components of the unit vector pointing along the line. A single unit step moves you l to the right, m forward and n upward.

<whisper>One value worth memorising outright</whisper> — a line equally inclined to all three axes has each direction cosine equal to plus or minus one over root three, because three l squared must equal one.
Nobody wants to compute three cosines from scratch every time. Direction ratios are the shortcut, and they are far easier to read off.
If a line passes through the points one, two, three and four, eight, eleven, the natural step along it is three, six, eight — just the coordinate differences.

Those numbers are not the direction cosines — their squares do not sum to one — but they are proportional to them. Any triple proportional to the direction cosines is a set of direction ratios. Think of it like a recipe given as a ratio.

To get the unique unit version, the direction cosines, you divide each ratio by the length root a squared plus b squared plus c squared. The single plus or minus reflects the two directions of the line.

An important asymmetry: direction ratios are never unique — two, three, minus one and four, six, minus two describe the same line. Only the direction cosines are unique, up to that single plus or minus.
Direction cosines belong to a directed line. Reverse the arrow and every sign flips together, which is exactly why the plus or minus keeps appearing.
One boundary case: the zero triple, zero, zero, zero, points nowhere and is meaningless as direction ratios. A valid set is never all zero.
Once you know a single point on a line and its direction, the line is completely determined — like knowing a train's starting station and the exact bearing of the track.

It pays to see how cleanly this separates two ideas. A line carries two completely independent pieces of information: where it is, given by any one point, and which way it goes, given by its direction.
The vector equation captures both. Position vector a supplies the where, direction b supplies the which way, and the parameter lambda slides you up and down the track.

Direction cosines and ratios capture only the which way, which is exactly why the same direction ratios describe infinitely many parallel lines scattered across space. To name one specific line, you must marry a direction to a point.

Eliminating lambda gives the Cartesian symmetric form: x minus x one over a, equals y minus y one over b, equals z minus z one over c. The denominators are the direction ratios; the constants are the point.
For a line through two points, the direction ratios are just the coordinate differences, so the two point form places those differences in the denominators.
Here is the geometry: start at the point a, and step any distance along the direction b. Every point on the line is reached for some value of lambda.

One caution baked into the form: lambda equals true distance from the base point only when b is a unit vector — that is, when its components are the direction cosines themselves. With arbitrary direction ratios, lambda is just a parameter, not a length.
A clean board level problem. A line has direction ratios two, minus three, six. Find its direction cosines, and write the equations of the line through one, four, minus two parallel to it.
First the length of the direction ratio triple: root of four plus nine plus thirty six, which is root forty nine, equal to seven.
Dividing each ratio by seven gives the direction cosines: two sevenths, minus three sevenths, six sevenths.
Always run the one second check: four over forty nine plus nine over forty nine plus thirty six over forty nine equals one. The normalisation is confirmed.
The vector equation places the point one, four, minus two as a, and the direction ratios two, minus three, six as b.
And the Cartesian equation simply reuses the direction ratios as denominators and the point's coordinates, with signs flipped, as the constants.
Notice the lesson: the equation of a line is, in effect, just its direction and one point written side by side.
This is a classic speed trap. A line makes sixty degrees with the x axis and forty five degrees with the y axis. What angle does it make with the z axis?
We do not need to find all the direction cosines. We can use the identity that the sum of the squared cosines of the three angles equals one, directly.
Substituting the two known angles: cos squared sixty plus cos squared forty five plus cos squared gamma equals one.
Cos squared sixty is one quarter and cos squared forty five is one half. So cos squared gamma is one quarter.
Taking the square root gives cos gamma equal to plus or minus one half. So gamma is sixty degrees or one hundred twenty degrees — both are valid.

So the speed move is simple: the instant a problem hands you cos squared gamma alone, reach for the plus or minus reflex and report both angles.
This links two skills. The points A, B and C are collinear. Find the unknown k, and then the direction cosines of the line.
Form the two direction ratio vectors from A. A B is minus two, four, two, and A C is two, k plus one, minus two.
Collinearity means these are proportional. The first and third ratios both equal minus one, which is consistent.
From the middle ratio, k plus one over four equals minus one, so k plus one is minus four, giving k equal to minus five.
Now use A B, which is minus two, four, two, with magnitude root twenty four, equal to two root six.

hava mein tedhe pakde do pencils sochiye. unke beech ka shortest gap ek teesri choti stick se bridge hota hai jo dono pencils ko right angle par milti hai. wo stick kis taraf point karegi? ek saath dono directions ke perpendicular.
aur dono directions ka cross product theek wahi common perpendicular banne ke liye bana hai. yahaan hai, dono lines ko bridge karta hua. gap d sirf isi direction ke saath napa jata hai.

to hum dono lines ko jodne wala koi bhi vector lete hain, unke reference points ke beech a two minus a one, aur sirf uska component us common perpendicular direction ke saath naapte hain. baaki sab tunnels ke saath chalta hai aur gap mein nahi gina jata.
vo projection shortest distance deta hai: joining vector ka cross product ke saath scalar triple product, us cross product ke size se divide kiya hua.

iska ek sundar matlab hai. scalar triple product un teen vectors par bane slanted box ka volume hai. us volume ko uske base ke area se, yaani cross product ke size se, divide kijiye aur aapko height milti hai — aur height hi perpendicular gap hai. Distance hai volume per unit base area.
to poori computation teen vector operations ki ek kadi hai: common perpendicular dhoondhne ke liye cross product, joining vector project karne ke liye dot product, aur khatam karne ke liye magnitude.

chunk_timeline.text: aage badhne se pehle, chaliye un kuch galtiyon ko pakka kar lete hain jo is poore section mein sabse aasan marks chhinati hain.
pehla, section formula ke weights. weight m far endpoint ko multiply karta hai, aur n near wale ko. inhen swap karna point ko poori tarah galat side par rakh deta hai.
doosra, negative ratio par ghabraiye mat. ratio ka negative answer galti nahi hai; ye bas batata hai ki cut segment ke baahar hai.
teesra, distance hamesha squared differences ke sum ka root hai — kabhi differences ke magnitudes ka sum nahin. na squaring chhodi ja sakti hai, na rooting.

chautha, collinearity ka additive distance test sirf tab kaam karta hai jab middle point sachmuch baaki dono ke beech ho. jab order pata na ho, proportional direction ratios par switch kijiye, jo kabhi ordering par nirbhar nahi karte.

paanchvaan, axis se distance ko plane se distance ke saath kabhi mat confuse kijiye. axis se distance shared coordinate chhodta hai aur root ke neeche do rakhta hai; plane se distance sirf wo ek zero wala coordinate rakhta hai.

aakhir mein, area aur volume magnitudes hain, to modulus par koi samjhauta nahi. aur ek quick sanity check — centroid ko apne triangle ke andar hi hona chahiye, to kisi vertex ke paar girta centroid arithmetic galti ka sanket hai.
yahaan space mein kisi line ke baare mein sabse zaroori sawaal hai — wo kahaan hai nahin, balki kis taraf point karti hai.
do dimensions mein ek angle kaafi tha. par space mein, kis taraf ko teenon axes ke against ek saath pin karna padta hai, to hum x, y aur z axes ke saath angles alpha, beta aur gamma naapte hain.
teen angles dhone ke bajay, hum unke cosines dhote hain: l hai cos alpha, m hai cos beta, n hai cos gamma. ye teen numbers line ke direction cosines hain.
Direction cosines ko ek budget baantne jaisa sochiye. Kisi direction ke paas kul strength one hoti hai, aur use wo strength teenon axes par kharch karni padti hai.
vo chhupa niyam jo ise budget banata hai vo hai master identity: l squared plus m squared plus n squared equals one. squares hamesha theek one mein jodte hain.

yahaan picture hai. line par origin se distance r par ek point P lijiye; har axis par uski shadow hai r times us axis ka cosine. to direction cosines har axis par kharch ki gayi length ke fractions hain.
ek yaad rakhne layak sentence mein: direction cosines line ke saath point karne wale unit vector ke components hain. ek unit step aapko l daain or, m aage aur n upar le jata hai.
ek value seedhe yaad kar lene layak — teenon axes ke barabar jhuki line ke har direction cosine ka maan hai plus ya minus one over root three, kyunki three l squared ko one ke barabar hona padta hai.
har baar teen cosines scratch se nikaalna koi nahi chahta. direction ratios wo shortcut hain, aur inhe padhna kahin aasan hai.
agar koi line points one, two, three aur four, eight, eleven se guzarti hai, to uske saath natural step hai three, six, eight — bas coordinate differences.

vo numbers direction cosines nahin hain — unke squares one mein nahin judte — par vo unke proportional hain. direction cosines ke proportional koi bhi triple ek set of direction ratios hai. ise ratio ke roop mein di gayi recipe jaisa sochiye.
Unique unit version, direction cosines, pane ke liye, har ratio ko length root a squared plus b squared plus c squared se divide kijiye. Wo ek plus ya minus line ki do directions dikhata hai.

ek zaroori asymmetry: direction ratios kabhi unique nahin hote — two, three, minus one aur four, six, minus two ek hi line batate hain. sirf direction cosines unique hote hain, us ek plus ya minus tak.
Direction cosines ek directed line ki hoti hain. arrow ulatiye aur har sign ek saath flip ho jata hai, yahi wajah hai ki plus ya minus baar-baar aata hai.
ek boundary case: zero triple, zero, zero, zero, kahin point nahin karta aur direction ratios ke roop mein meaningless hai. ek valid set kabhi poora zero nahin hota.
jaise hi aap kisi line par ek point aur uski direction jaan lete hain, line poori tarah tay ho jaati hai — jaise kisi train ka starting station aur track ka exact bearing jaan na.

ye dekhna faydemand hai ki ye kitni saafi se do ideas alag karta hai. ek line do poori tarah independent jaankariyaan dhoti hai: wo kahaan hai, kisi ek point se, aur wo kis taraf jaati hai, apni direction se.
Vector equation dono pakadta hai. position vector a deta hai kahan, direction b deta hai kis taraf, aur parameter lambda aapko track par aage-peechhe slide karta hai.

Direction cosines aur ratios sirf kis taraf pakadte hain, yahi wajah hai ki wahi direction ratios space mein bikhri anginat parallel lines batate hain. Kisi ek specific line ka naam lene ke liye, direction ko ek point se jodna padta hai.
Lambda ko hataane par Cartesian symmetric form milta hai: x minus x one over a, barabar y minus y one over b, barabar z minus z one over c. denominators direction ratios hain; constants point hai.
do points se guzarti line ke liye, direction ratios bas coordinate differences hain, to two point form un differences ko denominators mein rakhta hai.
yahaan geometry hai: point a se shuru kijiye, aur direction b ke saath koi bhi distance step kijiye. line ka har point kisi na kisi lambda ke liye mil jaata hai.

Form mein basi ek caution: lambda base point se true distance tabhi hota hai jab b ek unit vector ho — yaani jab uske components khud direction cosines hon. arbitrary direction ratios ke saath, lambda sirf ek parameter hai, length nahi.
ek saaf board level problem. ek line ke direction ratios hain two, minus three, six. iske direction cosines nikaaliye, aur one, four, minus two se guzarti iske parallel line ke equations likhiye.
pehle direction ratio triple ki length: root of chaar plus nau plus chhattis, yaani root untalees, barabar saat.
har ratio ko saat se divide karne par direction cosines milte hain: two sevenths, minus three sevenths, six sevenths.
hamesha one second ka check kijiye: four over untalis plus nau over untalis plus chhattis over untalis equals one. normalisation confirm ho gayi.
Vector equation point one, four, minus two ko a ke roop mein, aur direction ratios two, minus three, six ko b ke roop mein rakhta hai.
aur Cartesian equation bas direction ratios ko denominators ke roop mein aur point ke coordinates ko, signs flip karke, constants ke roop mein dobaara use karta hai.
sabak dhyan dijiye: kisi line ka equation asal mein bas uski direction aur ek point saath-saath likhe hote hain.
ye ek classic speed trap hai. ek line x axis ke saath saath degrees aur y axis ke saath paintalis degrees banati hai. wo z axis ke saath kaun sa angle banati hai?
humein saare direction cosines nikaalne ki zaroorat nahin. hum seedhe wo identity use kar sakte hain ki teenon angles ke squared cosines ka sum one hai.
donon known angles substitute karne par: cos squared saath plus cos squared paintalees plus cos squared gamma equals one.
Cos squared saath hai one quarter aur cos squared paintalees hai one half. To cos squared gamma hai one quarter.
Square root lene par cos gamma barabar plus ya minus one half. To gamma saath degrees ya ek sau bees degrees — dono valid hain.

yahaan trap hai — zyadaatar students saath degrees par rukkar mark kho dete hain. kyunki cos gamma barabar minus one half bhi equally valid hai, line plane ke neeche jhukkar ek sau bees degrees bana sakti hai. jaise hi cos squared akela dikhe, do answers likhiye.
to speed move simple hai: jis pal koi problem aapko cos squared gamma akela de, plus ya minus reflex uthaiye aur dono angles report kijiye.
ye do skills jodta hai. points A, B aur C collinear hain. unknown k nikaaliye, aur phir line ke direction cosines.
A se do direction ratio vectors banaiye. A B hai minus two, four, two, aur A C hai two, k plus one, minus two.
Collinearity ka matlab ye proportional hain. pehla aur teesra ratio dono minus one ke barabar hain, jo consistent hai.
beech wale ratio se, k plus one over four barabar minus one, to k plus one hai minus four, jo k ko minus five deta hai.
ab A B use kijiye, jo minus two, four, two hai, magnitude root choubis ke saath, barabar two root six.
har component ko two root six se divide karke simplify karne par direction cosines milte hain minus one over root six, two over root six, one over root six.

Cross check automatic hai: one sixth plus four sixths plus one sixth equals one. dhyan dijiye koi bhi scalar multiple direction ratios ke roop mein kaam aata; humne sirf aakhri step par normalise kiya — wo disciplined order jo cosines maange jaane par ratios report karne se bachata hai.

ek advanced problem. do lines ke direction cosines ek linear relation, three l plus m plus five n equals zero, aur ek quadratic relation ko satisfy karte hain. dono lines ke beech acute angle nikaaliye.
Linear relation se m ke liye solve kijiye: m barabar minus ka quantity three l plus five n. Phir ise quadratic mein substitute kijiye.
Substitute aur simplify karne ke baad, quadratic ghatkar l squared plus three l n plus two n squared equals zero banta hai, jo l plus n times l plus two n mein factor hota hai.
pehla factor l barabar minus n deta hai. linear relation mein wapas substitute karne par, pehli line ke direction ratios one, two, minus one ke proportional hain.
doosra factor l barabar minus two n deta hai, aur doosri line ke direction ratios two, minus one, minus one ke proportional hain. dono vectors ka magnitude root six hai.
Angle ka cosine hai dot product over magnitudes ka product: two minus two plus one, over six, yaani one sixth. To theta hai inverse cosine of one sixth, kareeb assi degrees.

do takeaways: ek linear plus ek quadratic relation aam taur par do directions nikaalta hai, yahi wajah hai sawaal do lines ka zikr karta hai. aur humein kabhi actual direction cosines ki zaroorat nahi padi, kyunki angle formula scale free hai.
chaliye is subtopic ko un traps pakka karke band karte hain jo examiners direction cosines aur line equations ke aaspaas baar-baar lagate hain.
pehla, sabse common blunder — direction ratios ko answer likh dena bina unki length se divide kiye. jab bhi cosines maange jayein, hamesha normalisation step ke saath khatm kijiye.

doosra, plus ya minus kabhi mat bhuliye. ek undirected line ke do opposite direction cosine sets hote hain, aur jo problems kisi angle ke cos squared tak pahunchte hain unke aam taur par do valid angle answers hote hain.
teesra, kisi line ke axis ke saath angle aur us axis ke perpendicular plane ke saath angle ko mat confuse kijiye. wo complementary hain, equal nahin.

paanchvaan, parameter lambda ko distance mat samjhiye. lambda true length tabhi hai jab direction vector ek unit vector ho — yaani jab aapne raw ratios ke bajay direction cosines use kiye hon.

aur ek one second ki aadat jo poori problems bachati hai: har direction cosine answer ke baad, teenon values square kijiye aur confirm kijiye sum one hai. agar nahi, to aap normalise karna bhool gaye.

board_events.text: Know which configuration you are in first
Two lines can intersect, be parallel, or be skew.
Combine the triple product with a glance at whether $\vec{b}_1,\vec{b}_2$ are proportional.
Shortest distance $=0$ is the working definition of the lines meeting.
The reported acute angle always lies in $[0^{\circ},90^{\circ}]$ — a sanity bound.
Angle between two given lines in symmetric form
A negative dot product would still give $\theta=\cos^{-1}\tfrac{4}{9}$ after the modulus.
Only the acute angle carries meaning for a pair of lines.
Two fast tests — no full angle needed
(a) DRs $(2,-1,1)$ and $(1,1,-1)$: perpendicularity needs one dot product.
(b) $(3,p,2)$ parallel to $(6,-4,4)$: parallelism needs ratio equality.
Dot product $=0$ means perpendicular; equal ratios mean parallel — never swap them.
A reliable habit: write the dot product first, then check proportionality only if needed.
Shortest distance in vector form
Check: $(6,-6,3)$ is perpendicular to both directions (both dots $=0$).
Find $k$ so two lines are coplanar, then their meeting point
Coplanarity is a single scalar equation — one special $k$ makes the pair meet.
The slips that cost distance-and-angle marks
Never drop the modulus in the angle formula.
Do not swap the perpendicular and parallel tests.
Do not use the skew formula on parallel lines — the cross product dies.
Keep the modulus on the triple product; recognise coplanar $\iff$ STP $=0$.
Compute $\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2$ first — its size and its zero-ness both inform you.
Every distance answer must be $\ge 0$; a negative result means a missing modulus.
The flattest surface in space
The direction it faces is the normal vector $\vec n$ — tilt it and the whole plane tilts.

board_events.text: Notice: every formula here is built from the normal $\vec n$.

segments.text: Before computing anything, it pays to know which of three situations you are in, because each behaves differently.

Two distinct lines can intersect, sharing exactly one point, so the shortest distance is zero; they can be parallel, the same direction, never meeting, with a constant gap; or they can be skew, different directions yet still never meeting.
One quantity separates the cases cleanly. The scalar triple product is zero for intersecting and parallel lines, because both are coplanar, and non zero exactly for skew lines.

Combine that triple product with a glance at whether the two directions are proportional, and all three cases are told apart with no heavy algebra: proportional directions plus zero triple product means parallel, non proportional plus zero means intersecting, and non zero means skew.

For parallel lines the skew formula fails, because the cross product of the shared direction with itself is zero. Instead, since they never tilt, the gap is the same everywhere: the perpendicular distance from any one point of one line to the other.

And keep this in mind: if the shortest distance comes out zero, the lines are not skew at all — they intersect. Shortest distance equals zero is the working definition of the lines meeting, and it is the same as the coplanarity condition.

One useful bound to close on: once the modulus is applied, the reported angle always lies between zero and ninety degrees. A line with itself gives zero, perpendicular lines give ninety, and the value never strays outside that band.
A clean board level angle problem. We want the acute angle between two lines given in symmetric form, so we read off their direction ratios first.
From the denominators, the first line has direction ratios two, minus one, two, and the second has one, two, two.
The dot product is two times one, plus minus one times two, plus two times two — that is two minus two plus four, equals four.
Each magnitude is root nine, which is three.
So the cosine of the angle is the size of four over three times three, which is four ninths. The acute angle is the inverse cosine of four ninths.

Notice: had the dot product come out negative, say minus four, the modulus would still return the same acute angle. The equations describe the same pair of lines whichever way you walk along them, so only the acute angle carries meaning.
That is the whole lesson of the modulus here: for a pair of lines, direction is reversible, so we always report the sharp, acute angle between them.
This speed trap has two parts. Part a asks us to show two lines are perpendicular; part b asks us to find a parameter that makes two lines parallel.
For part a, perpendicularity needs only a single dot product — no angle computation at all. The direction ratios are two, minus one, one and one, one, minus one.
The dot product is two minus one minus one, which is zero. A zero dot product means the lines are perpendicular. We are done — no need to touch the cosine formula.
For part b, parallelism needs only ratio equality. We set the ratios of corresponding components of three, p, two and six, minus four, four equal.
Three over six and two over four both equal one half. So p over minus four equals one half, giving p equal to minus two.

Lock it in: dot product equals zero means perpendicular, and equal ratios mean parallel. The trap is reaching for the full cosine formula for part a, or mixing up the two tests. Write the dot product first — if it is zero you are finished.

So build a reliable habit: write the dot product first. If it is zero, the lines are perpendicular and you stop. Only if it is not zero is it worth checking proportionality for parallelism or computing a full angle.
Now a full shortest distance computation between two skew lines given in vector form. We read the reference points and directions from each.
The first line has reference point one, two, minus one and direction two, one, minus two. The second has reference point three, minus one, one and direction one, two, two.
First the common perpendicular: the cross product of the two directions is six, minus six, three, whose magnitude is root eighty one, equal to nine. Compute this first — its size is your denominator.
The joining vector between reference points is two, minus three, two.
The scalar triple product is two times six, plus minus three times minus six, plus two times three — that is twelve plus eighteen plus six, equals thirty six.
So the shortest distance is the size of thirty six over nine, which is four units.

A quick check that we projected along the genuine common perpendicular: six, minus six, three dotted with each direction gives zero, confirming it is perpendicular to both lines. Cross product, then dot product, then magnitude — three operations chained into one distance.
An advanced problem. We must find the value of k for which two lines are coplanar, and then locate their point of intersection.
We apply the coplanarity determinant. The joining vector is minus one, k minus one, three, and the two directions are one, two, three and three, two, one.
Coplanarity means this three by three determinant, with the joining vector on top and the two directions below, equals zero.
Expanding along the first row and simplifying, the whole determinant collapses to eight k minus sixteen.
Setting that to zero gives eight k equals sixteen, so k equals two.

With k equal to two, write general points on each line and equate coordinates. Solving the linear system gives the parameters three quarters and five quarters, and the intersection point is thirteen quarters, seven halves, eleven quarters.

Let's lock in the traps that examiners set around angles and shortest distances between lines.

First, never drop the modulus in the angle formula. A negative dot product yields an obtuse value, but the angle between two lines is always reported acute. And you must divide by both magnitudes — forgetting the denominator can even give a cosine bigger than one.

Second, do not swap the two tests. Perpendicular means the dot product is zero; parallel means the ratios are equal. Students routinely apply the wrong one — checking proportionality when they meant perpendicularity.

Third, never use the skew distance formula on parallel lines. When the directions are proportional, their cross product is the zero vector and the formula divides by zero. Switch to the parallel line formula instead.

Fourth, distance is never negative, so keep the modulus on the scalar triple product even though the product itself can be negative. And remember that show the lines intersect is the very same task as show the determinant is zero.

And one last sanity check: every distance answer must be at least zero. A negative result is impossible and simply means you forgot a modulus somewhere along the way.
A plane is the flattest, most unbending surface in space — an infinite tabletop. The remarkable thing is how little it takes to fix one: a single point on it, plus the direction it faces.

The direction a plane faces is captured by a vector sticking straight out of the surface, the normal vector n. Tilt the normal and the whole tabletop tilts with it; slide the point and it slides parallel to itself.

Here is the picture. Stand a pencil upright on a sheet of glass — the pencil is the normal, the glass is the plane. Any point R lies on the glass exactly when the arrow from the base point A to R runs flat along the glass, perpendicular to the pencil.
Perpendicular means the dot product is zero, which gives the master equation of a plane in one stroke: r minus a, dotted with n, equals zero — or, tidied up, r dot n equals a constant d.

Every form of the plane equation is just this idea in different clothes. Given three points instead of a normal, build two edge vectors and cross them — the cross product is perpendicular to both edges, so you have manufactured a normal out of thin air.
Even the intercept form, with intercepts a, b, c on the axes, is just three points in disguise — the three axis crossings.

One caution on the normal form. Writing r dot n hat equals p gives p as the true distance from the origin only when n hat is a unit vector and p is non negative. Otherwise p is not the origin distance.

The angle between two planes is simply the angle between their normals. Two surfaces compare like two arrows, so we use the cosine of the angle between the normals.

But the line and plane case hides a twist. When a line meets a plane, the angle we care about is measured against the surface, not against the normal — and the normal sticks up at ninety degrees to the surface.
Here it is. If alpha is the angle between the line and the normal, then the angle phi we want, between the line and the surface, is its complement — ninety degrees minus alpha.

Cosine of the complement is sine, so the line plane angle uses a sine: sin phi equals the modulus of b dot n, over the product of magnitudes. Forgetting this single sine cosine swap is the most common mistake on the entire topic.

So carry this hook: plane to plane uses cosine, line to plane uses sine. Two surfaces compare like two arrows with cosine; a line piercing a surface is measured against the flat, which flips cosine to sine.

And the normals decide everything else too. Two planes are parallel when their normals are proportional, and perpendicular when the normals dot to zero. A line lies in or is parallel to a plane when its direction dots the normal to zero.
To find the distance of a point from a plane, drop a perpendicular and measure along the normal. The formula is beautifully mechanical.
You simply feed the point into the plane expression and divide by the length of the normal. The modulus is there because distance cannot be negative.
But the sign of that expression, before you take the modulus, actually tells you which side of the plane the point is on — a fact that solves a whole class of problems for free.

Evaluate the plane expression at two points. If both give the same sign, the points lie on the same side; if the signs differ, the plane separates them, and the segment joining them must cross the plane.

For two parallel planes, the gap follows the same recipe: the difference of the constants over the length of the shared normal. But you must scale both planes to identical normals first, or the constants are not comparable.

A recurring slip: the distance divides by the length of the normal, root a squared plus b squared plus c squared — not by its square. Dropping the square root, or squaring the denominator, both give the wrong number.

So the side test is essentially free: to decide whether the origin, or any point, lies on the same side as another, just compare the signs of the plane expression — no extra computation beyond what the distance already required.
When a problem says the plane through the line where two planes meet, do not find that line. There is a far more elegant shortcut.
Instead write P one plus lambda P two equals zero. Every choice of lambda is automatically a plane through that intersection line, and one extra condition pins down the single right lambda.

Geometrically, this is a pencil of planes — an infinite book of pages all hinged along the same spine, which is the intersection line. Sweeping lambda across all real values flips through every page of the book.
The extra condition simply selects the one page you need. A point to pass through, or a plane to be perpendicular to, becomes a single linear equation in lambda.
If the condition is a point lying on the plane, substitute that point into the family and solve for lambda. That is it — no system of simultaneous equations and no parametrisation of the line.

One limit to remember: the form P one plus lambda P two can never reproduce P two itself, since no finite lambda gives it. If the correct answer happens to be P two, use the symmetric form, mu times P one plus P two, to recover it.

And if the condition is being perpendicular to a given plane, set the dot product of the family's normal with that plane's normal to zero. Whatever the condition, it collapses to one equation in lambda.
Let's gather every plane formula before we start solving.
The point normal form, where the coefficients are the normal and the fixed values are the point.
The three point determinant form, and the intercept form for a plane meeting the axes at a, b, c.
The family of planes through a line of intersection — fix lambda with one extra condition.
The plane to plane angle uses cosine of the normals; the line to plane angle uses sine. Remember: plane to plane cosine, line to plane sine.

Notice the thread running through the whole board: every single formula here is built from the normal. That is why identifying the normal is always the efficient first move on a plane question.

Plane expression ko do points par evaluate kijiye. Agar dono same sign den, points ek hi side par hain; agar signs alag hon, plane unhein alag karta hai, aur unhein jodne wala segment plane ko cross karna hi padta hai.

do parallel planes ke liye, gap wahi recipe follow karta hai: constants ka difference shared normal ki length par. par aapko pehle dono planes ko identical normals par scale karna hoga,varna constants comparable nahin hain.

ek baar-baar hone wali galti: distance normal ki length se divide hoti hai, root a squared plus b squared plus c squared — uske square se nahi. square root girana, ya denominator square karna, dono galat number dete hain.

to side test asal mein free hai: ye tay karne ke liye ki origin, ya koi point, doosre ke same side par hai ya nahi, bas plane expression ke signs ki tulna kijiye — distance ne jo pehle hi maanga usse zyada koi computation nahi.
jab koi problem kahe us line se guzarta plane jahan do planes milte hain, us line ko mat dhoondhiye. ek kahin zyada elegant shortcut hai.
iske bajay P one plus lambda P two equals zero likhiye. lambda ka har choice apne aap us intersection line se guzarta ek plane hai, aur ek extra condition us ek sahi lambda ko tay kar deta hai.

Geometrically, ye ek pencil of planes hai — pages ki ek anant kitaab jo sab ek hi spine par hinged hain, wo spine intersection line hai. lambda ko saari real values par sweep karna kitaab ke har page ko palat deta hai.
Extra condition bas wo ek page chunta hai jo aapko chahiye. Kisi point se guzarna, ya kisi plane ke perpendicular hona, lambda mein ek single linear equation ban jata hai.

agar condition hai koi point plane par ho, to us point ko family mein substitute karke lambda ke liye solve kijiye. bas — koi simultaneous equations ka system nahi aur line ka koi parametrisation nahi.

yaad rakhne layak ek limit: P one plus lambda P two form kabhi P two ko khud reproduce nahin kar sakta, kyunki koi finite lambda wo nahin deta. agar sahi answer P two hi ho, to use paane ke liye symmetric form, mu times P one plus P two, use kijiye.

aur agar condition hai kisi diye plane ke perpendicular hona, to family ke normal ka us plane ke normal ke saath dot product zero rakhiye. condition jo bhi ho, wo lambda mein ek equation mein ghat jaati hai.
chaliye solve shuru karne se pehle har plane formula ikattha kar lete hain.
Point normal form, jahan coefficients normal hain aur fixed values point.
Three point determinant form, aur intercept form us plane ke liye jo axes ko a, b, c par mile.
Line of intersection se guzarti planes ki family — ek extra condition se lambda tay kijiye.
Plane to plane angle normals ka cosine use karta hai; line to plane angle sine. Yaad rakhiye: plane to plane cosine, line to plane sine.
Point to plane distance, aur parallel plane distance dono ko equal normals par scale karne ke baad. Dono normal ki length se divide hoti hain.
poore board mein chalta dhaaga dhyaan dijiye: yahaan ka har ek formula normal se bana hai. isiliye kisi plane sawaal par normal pehchanna hamesha efficient pehla kadam hai.

chunk_timeline.text: kuch bhi compute karne se pehle, ye jaan na faydemand hai ki aap teen mein se kis situation mein hain, kyunki har ek alag tarah se behave karti hai.

do alag lines intersect kar sakti hain, theek ek point saanjha karte hue, to shortest distance zero; wo parallel ho sakti hain, same direction, kabhi na milte hue, constant gap ke saath; ya wo skew ho sakti hain, alag directions par phir bhi kabhi na milte hue.
ek quantity cases ko saafi se alag karti hai. scalar triple product intersecting aur parallel lines ke liye zero hota hai, kyunki dono coplanar hain, aur theek skew lines ke liye non zero.

us triple product ko is nazar ke saath milaiye ki dono directions proportional hain ya nahi, aur teenon cases bina bhaari algebra ke alag ho jaati hain: proportional directions plus zero triple product ka matlab parallel, non proportional plus zero ka matlab intersecting, aur non zero ka matlab skew.

Parallel lines ke liye skew formula fail ho jata hai, kyunki shared direction ka khud ke saath cross product zero hai. Iske bajay, chuki wo kabhi tilt nahi karti, gap har jagah same hai: ek line ke kisi bhi ek point ki doosri se perpendicular distance.

aur ye yaad rakhiye: agar shortest distance zero aaye, to lines skew hain hi nahi — wo intersect karti hain. shortest distance equals zero lines ke milne ki working definition hai, aur ye coplanarity condition ke barabar hai.

band karne ke liye ek upyogi bound: modulus lagne ke baad, reported angle hamesha zero aur nabbe degrees ke beech hota hai. ek line khud ke saath zero deti hai, perpendicular lines nabbe, aur value kabhi us band ke baahar nahi jaati.
ek saaf board level angle problem. humein symmetric form mein di gayi do lines ke beech acute angle chahiye, to hum pehle unke direction ratios padhte hain.
Denominators se, pehli line ke direction ratios hain two, minus one, two, aur doosri ke one, two, two.
Dot product hai two times one, plus minus one times two, plus two times two — yaani two minus two plus four, barabar chaar.
har magnitude root nau hai, yaani teen.
to angle ka cosine hai chaar ka size, teen times teen par, yaani four ninths. acute angle hai inverse cosine of four ninths.

dhyan dijiye: agar dot product negative aata, jaise minus four, to bhi modulus wahi acute angle lautata. equations unhi lines ki jodi batate hain chahe aap kisi bhi taraf chalein, to sirf acute angle ka matlab hota hai.
yahi yahaan modulus ka poora sabak hai: lines ki jodi ke liye, direction ulti ja sakti hai, to hum hamesha unke beech ka sharp, acute angle report karte hain.
is speed trap ke do hisse hain. hissa a kehta hai do lines ko perpendicular dikhaiye; hissa b kehta hai wo parameter nikaliye jo do lines ko parallel banaye.
hissa a ke liye, perpendicularity ko sirf ek dot product chahiye — koi angle computation nahi. direction ratios hain two, minus one, one aur one, one, minus one.
Dot product hai two minus one minus one, yaani zero. zero dot product ka matlab lines perpendicular hain. ho gaya — cosine formula ko chhoone ki zaroorat nahi.
hissa b ke liye, parallelism ko sirf ratio equality chahiye. hum three, p, two aur six, minus four, four ke corresponding components ke ratios barabar rakhte hain.
Three over six aur two over four dono one half ke barabar hain. To p over minus four barabar one half, jo p ko minus two deta hai.

pakka kijiye: dot product barabar zero ka matlab perpendicular, aur equal ratios ka matlab parallel. trap hai hissa a ke liye poora cosine formula uthana, ya dono tests ko gaddamadd karna. pehle dot product likhiye — agar zero hai to aap khatam.

to ek reliable aadat banaiye: pehle dot product likhiye. agar zero hai, lines perpendicular hain aur aap ruk jaate hain. sirf agar zero na ho, tabhi parallelism ke liye proportionality check karna ya poora angle nikaalna worth hai.
ab vector form mein di gayi do skew lines ke beech poori shortest distance computation. hum har ek se reference points aur directions padhte hain.
pehli line ka reference point one, two, minus one aur direction two, one, minus two. doosri ka reference point three, minus one, one aur direction one, two, two.
pehle common perpendicular: dono directions ka cross product hai six, minus six, three, jiska magnitude root ikyaasi hai, barabar nau. ise pehle compute kijiye — iska size aapka denominator hai.
Reference points ke beech joining vector hai two, minus three, two.
Scalar triple product hai two times six, plus minus three times minus six, plus two times three — yaani baarah plus athaarah plus chhah, barabar chhattis.
to shortest distance hai chhattis ka size nau par, yaani chaar units.

ek quick check ki humne asli common perpendicular ke saath project kiya: six, minus six, three ko har direction ke saath dot karne par zero milta hai, jo confirm karta hai ye dono lines ke perpendicular hai. cross product, fir dot product, fir magnitude — teen operations ek distance mein judi.
ek advanced problem. humein wo k nikaalna hai jiske liye do lines coplanar hon, aur phir unka point of intersection dhoondhna hai.
ham coplanarity determinant lagate hain. joining vector hai minus one, k minus one, three, aur dono directions one, two, three aur three, two, one.
Coplanarity ka matlab ye three by three determinant, upar joining vector aur neeche dono directions ke saath, zero ke barabar ho.
pehli row ke saath expand karke simplify karne par, poora determinant ghatkar eight k minus solah banta hai.
use zero rakhne par eight k barabar solah, to k barabar do.

K barabar do ke saath, har line par general points likhkar coordinates barabar kijiye. linear system solve karne par parameters three quarters aur five quarters milte hain, aur intersection point hai thirteen quarters, seven halves, eleven quarters.
gahara idea: coplanarity ek single scalar equation hai, triple product, to line pairs ki one parameter family mein theek wahi khaas k hota hai jo unhein milata hai.

doosra, dono tests swap mat kijiye. perpendicular ka matlab dot product zero; parallel ka matlab ratios barabar. students aksar galat wala laga dete hain — perpendicularity ke liye proportionality check kar baithte hain.

aur ek aakhiri sanity check: har distance answer kam se kam zero hona chahiye. negative result asambhav hai aur bas itna batata hai ki aap kahin raste mein ek modulus bhool gaye.

ek plane space mein sabse flat, sabse na jhukne wali surface hai — ek anant tabletop. kamaal ki baat ye hai ki ek ko tay karne mein kitna kam lagta hai: us par ek point, plus wo jis direction ko face karta hai.

Forms come from a normal; distance divides by the normal's length.

A built-in check: $\sin\varphi=\tfrac{16}{21}<1$, as any genuine sine must be.

Scale parallel planes to identical normals before comparing constants.
In family problems, never solve for the intersection line — write $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$.
The normal is everything: forms, angles, and distances all flow from it.
Almost every nearest, foot, or image question is one act
Three things appear at once: the foot F, the distance PF, and the image P'.
These are three readings of one drawing, not three separate topics.
Which of the three a question asks for is almost cosmetic — the work is identical.
Only the way you find the foot differs between the line case and the plane case.
